units.la: DISPUTATIONIS ONTOSOPHICAE PARS ALTERA.
units.tr: Part Two of the Ontosophical Disputation

units.la: Actenus de Relatione Originis inter Principium & Principiatum, inter Causam & Effectum; sequitur Relatio Negationis, orta quoque ex ipsa rerum multitudine; eaque vel inter Diversa, vel inter Priora & Posteriora. Relatio quae est inter Diversa, vocatur Distinctio, eique opponitur Identitas. Relatio vero inter Priora & Posteriora Ordo vocatur. Distinctio ad relationem negationis refertur, quia Distinctio formaliter in negatione consistit, per quam unum non est aliud quam vis nonnulli Distinctionem in Pofitivam & Negativam distinguant, & Positivam vocent eam, ubi utrumque extremorum est positivum; Negativam autem, ubi alterum, extremorum est negativum. Sed ubi utrumque extremorum est negativum: exempli gratiâ Cæcitas & Surditas, ibi semper concipitur subjectum aliquod positivum, cui ejusmodi negationes vel privationes tribuuntur.
units.tr: So far I have spoken of the Relation of Origin between Principle and Principiate, between Cause and Effect. There follows the Relation of Negation, which also arises from the very multiplicity of things. This relation holds either between Diverse things or between Prior and Posterior things. The relation between Diverse things is called Distinction, and Identity is opposed to it. The relation between Prior and Posterior things is called Order. Distinction is referred to the relation of negation, because Distinction formally consists in negation, by which one thing is not another. Some divide Distinction into Positive and Negative, calling it Positive when both extremes are positive, but Negative when one of the extremes is negative. Where both extremes are negative, for example Blindness and Deafness, there is always conceived some positive subject to which such negations or privations are attributed.

units.la: Distinctio Positiva triplex est, Realis, Modalis, & Rationis: Ea autem, inter quæ Distinctio Positiva intercedit, uno nomine Distincta vocantur, quæ sunt vel Diversa vel Opposita, hæcque vel Disparata vel Contraria; & hæc iterum vel Relata sive relativè opposita, vel vel Adversa, quæ vulgò etiam Contraria dicuntur. Distinctio Negativa locum habet, ubi alterum extremum est non ens, scilicet in Contradicentibus & Privantibus. Distinctio Realis est ea, quæ reperitur inter duo aut plura entia completa, vel inter duas aut plures substantias, vel inter modum unius substantiæ & inter modum alterius substantiæ, vel verò inter unam substantiam & modum alterius substantiæ. Hæc autem Distinctio Realis ex eo cognoscitur, quòd substantiam unam clarè & distinctè intelligere possumus sine alia substantia: vel quia modi illi, quos realiter distingui dicimus, clarè & distinctè intelligi nequeunt sine substantiis illis realiter distinctis, quarum sunt modi. Deum agnoscentes certisumus, ipsum posse efficere, quicquid clarè & distinctè intelligimus, & si vel maximè Deus tàm arctè duas res sibi mutuò univisset, ut nunquam essent separandæ, non tamen inde sequeretur, eas non esse realiter distinctas, quia potentiâ, quam habuisset eos separandi, se ipsum non privasset.
units.tr: Positive Distinction is threefold: Real, Modal, and of Reason. Those things between which Positive Distinction holds are called by one name Distinct. They are either Diverse or Opposed, and these are either Disparate or Contrary; and these again are either Related, that is, relatively opposed, or Adverse, which are commonly also called Contrary. Negative Distinction takes place where the other extreme is a non-being, namely in Contradictories and Privatives. Real Distinction is that which is found between two or more complete beings, or between two or more substances, or between the mode of one substance and the mode of another substance, or between one substance and the mode of another substance. This Real Distinction is recognized from the fact that we can clearly and distinctly understand one substance without another substance, or because those modes which we say are really distinct cannot be clearly and distinctly understood without those really distinct substances of which they are modes. Acknowledging God, we are certain that he can bring about whatever we clearly and distinctly understand. Even if God had so closely joined two things to each other that they could never be separated, it would not follow that they are not really distinct, because he would not thereby have deprived himself of the power he would have had to separate them.

units.la: 72. Distinctio Modalis ea vocatur, in qua vel alterutra vel utraque pars distinctionis est modus, & proindè duplex est: alia scilicet inter modum propriè dictum & inter substantiam, cujus est modus: alia verò inter duos modos ejusdem substantiæ: Prior ex eo cognoscitur, quod possimus quidem substantiam clarè percipere absque modo, quem ab illa distinguimus, sed non possimus vice versa modum illum intelligere sine substantia. Posterior verò ex eo cognoscitur, quod unum quidem modum absque alio possimus cognoscere, ac vice versa, sed neutrum tamen sine eadem substantia, cui insunt. Distinctio verò inter modum unius substantiæ & inter modum alterius substantiæ pertinet ad distinctionem realem. Distinctio quæ est inter modos subsistendi ab essentia divina in SS. Trinitate & inter Modos ipsos talis est, cui similis in tota rerum natura non reperitur. Eam ergò ut ab aliis distinctionibus distinguamus, cum quibusdam Personalem vocare malumus, quàm mysterium hoc ad communes distinctionis leges revocare.
units.tr: 72. Modal Distinction is that in which either one or both parts of the distinction is a mode, and it is therefore twofold. One kind is between a mode properly so called and the substance of which it is a mode. The other is between two modes of the same substance. The former is recognized from the fact that we can indeed clearly perceive the substance without the mode which we distinguish from it, but cannot conversely understand that mode without the substance. The latter is recognized from the fact that we can know one mode without the other, and vice versa, but neither without the same substance in which they inhere. The distinction between a mode of one substance and a mode of another substance, however, belongs to real distinction. The distinction which holds between the modes of subsisting from the divine essence in the Holy Trinity and the Modes themselves is of such a kind that nothing like it is found in the whole of nature. Therefore, in order to distinguish it from other distinctions, we prefer, with some, to call it Personal, rather than to reduce this mystery to the common laws of distinction.

units.la: Distinctio Rationis est ea, quam facit ipsa ratio: estque triplex. Prima est inter substantiam & aliquod ejus attributum, sine quo ipsa intelligi nequit, h. e. primarium & essentiale, quod ipsam rei essentiam constituit: & ex eo cognoscitur, quod non possimus claram & distinctam substantiæ illius ideam formare, si ab ea attributum illud excludamus. Secunda est inter duo attributa ejusdem substantiæ essentialia: & ex eo cognoscitur, quód non possim illorum attributorum unum clarè & distinctè intelligere, quin simul alterum quoque clarè & distinctè intelligam. Tertia est inter modos cogitandi, quos tanquàm in objectis consideramus, qui ratione tantùm differunt tùm ab objectis, de quibus cogitamus, tùm à se mutuò in uno eodemque objecto: atque huc pertinent omnes Notiones Logicæ ac varij considerandi modi. Vulgò Distinctio Rationis est vel Rationis Ratiocinantis, quando ratio vel mens absque ullo fundamento ratiocinando tantùm distinctionem aliquam fingit: vel Rationis ratiocinatæ, quando mens seu ratio in eadem re distinguit varias rationes formales, ita quidem ut res sit eadem, sed virtute multiplex, unde Distinctio Virtualis vocatur: ita in una eaq; simplicissima essentia divina mens nostra distinguit varia attributa, nec sine aliquo fundamento proprer diversitatem scilicet objectorum & effectorum.
units.tr: Distinction of Reason is that which reason itself makes, and it is threefold. The first is between a substance and some attribute of it without which it cannot be understood, that is, an attribute which is primary and essential and constitutes the very essence of the thing. It is recognized from the fact that we cannot form a clear and distinct idea of that substance if we exclude that attribute from it. The second is between two essential attributes of the same substance; it is recognized from the fact that I cannot clearly and distinctly understand one of those attributes without at the same time clearly and distinctly understanding the other. The third is between modes of thinking, which we consider as if they were in objects, and which differ only by reason, both from the objects of which we think and from one another within one and the same object. To this belong all Logical Notions and the various modes of considering. Commonly, Distinction of Reason is either that of reasoning reason, when reason or mind, reasoning without any foundation, merely feigns some distinction; or that of reasoned reason, when the mind or reason distinguishes in the same thing various formal reasons, so that the thing is indeed one but manifold in power, whence it is called Virtual Distinction. Thus our mind, in the one and most simple divine essence, distinguishes various attributes, and not without some foundation, namely the diversity of objects and effects.

units.la: Distinctionis oppositum Convenientia vocatur, per quam plura aut quasi plura inter se in aliquo tertio reali consentiunt: unde ratio formalis Convenientiæ est ipsa Concordantia unius extremi cum alio, quæ si tanta sit, ut extrema essentiam habeant unam & eandem, Identitas proprie nominatur, qui summus est convenientiæ gradus. Omnis autem Identitas, quæ rebus tribuitur, requirit aliquod fundamentum, quod revera vel apparenter manet immutatum. Sicut autem Differentia vulgo in Numericam, Specificam & Genericam distinguitur: ita Identitas alia est Numerica, alia Specifica, alia Generica.
units.tr: The opposite of Distinction is called Agreement, by which several things, or things as it were several, agree with one another in some third real thing. The formal reason of Agreement is the very concordance of one extreme with another. If this concordance is so great that the extremes have one and the same essence, it is properly called Identity, which is the highest degree of agreement. Every Identity that is attributed to things requires some foundation which really or apparently remains unchanged. Just as Difference is commonly divided into Numerical, Specific and Generic, so Identity is either Numerical, Specific or Generic.

units.la: Ex rerum distinctione oritur Ordo vel Confusio. Ordo est enim distinctorum debita inter se dispositio. Confusio autem est ejusdem ordinis permutatio. Ordo locum habet vel inter ea quæ sunt priora vel posteriora, vel inter ea quæ sunt simul. Ibi est Subordinatio, hic vero Coordinatio. Non quælibet mixtura Confusionem infert, contrarium enim patet ex mixtura colorum in picturis, & ex mixtura sonorum in cantu. Sed Confusio talis est ordinis permutatio, qua vel prius est, quod deberet esse posterius, vel posterius, quod deberet esse prius, vel ubi priora aut posteriora sunt, quæ deberent esse simul, vel ubi simul sunt, quorum unum altero deberet esse vel prius vel posterius.
units.tr: From the distinction of things arises Order or Confusion. Order is the due arrangement of distinct things among themselves; Confusion is a permutation of that same order. Order has its place either among those things which are prior or posterior, or among those which are simultaneous. Here there is Subordination, there Coordination. Not every mixture produces confusion; the contrary is plain from the mixture of colours in paintings and of sounds in music. But Confusion is such a permutation of order by which either what ought to be posterior is prior, or what ought to be prior is posterior, or where there are things prior or posterior which ought to be simultaneous, or where things are simultaneous, one of which ought to be either prior or posterior to the other.

units.la: Ordo in rebus variis modis considerari potest, unde totidem etiam modis aliquid prius & posterius vel etiam simul esse dicimus, scilicet respectu I. vel dispositionis, 2. vel durationis, 3. vel dignitatis, 4. vel cognitionis, 5. vel naturæ. Ordo Dispositionis respicit 1. vel locum, ita dispositione prius nominatur illud, quod aliud loco præcedit, & posterius illud, quod aliud loco sequitur. 2. vel methodum & cognoscendi viam. Ordo Durationis respicit tempus: ita tempore vel duratione prius nominatur, quod tempore aliud antecedit: quod verò tempore alteri succedit, vocatur duratione posterius: hinc distinctio inter Successivum & Simultaneum. e. g. Polygamia est vel Successiva vel Simultanea: huc etiam pertinet distinctio inter Simultatem potentia & potentiam simultatis. Ordo dignitatis statuitur 1. vel ratione substantia: ita Deus angelo, angelus mente humana, mens corpore est nobilior. 2. vel ratione accidentium, ita formosus dignior est deformi: 3. vel ratione utilitatis nostra: ita panis dignior est carne. 4. vel ratione æstimationis & opinionis humana, quomodò rerum dignitas pro hominum opinione sæpè variat.
units.tr: Order can be considered in things in various ways, and in as many ways we say that something is prior and posterior, or even simultaneous: namely with respect to (1) disposition, (2) duration, (3) dignity, (4) cognition, (5) nature. The Order of Disposition regards (1) place: thus that which precedes another in place is called prior in disposition, and that which follows another in place posterior. It regards (2) method and the way of knowing. The Order of Duration regards time: thus that which precedes another in time is called prior in time or duration; but that which succeeds another in time is called posterior in duration. Hence the distinction between Successive and Simultaneous; e.g. polygamy is either successive or simultaneous. To this also belongs the distinction between simultaneity of power and power of simultaneity. The Order of Dignity is established (1) by reason of substance: thus God is nobler than an angel, an angel than the human mind, the mind than the body; (2) by reason of accidents: thus a handsome person is worthier than an ugly one; (3) by reason of our usefulness: thus bread is worthier than meat; (4) by reason of human estimation and opinion, as the dignity of things often varies according to the opinion of men.

units.la: 77. Ordo cognitionis petitur 1. vel à natura rerum: ita causæ effectus, simplicia compositis, cognitione priora sunt. 2. vel à cognitione nostra distincta & facili: ita mens prius cognoscitur quàm corpus. 3. vel à vulgari consuetudine: ita sensibilia prius cognoscuntur quàm intellectualia. Prius ergò ergò cognitione est, quod ante aliud cognoscitur: Posterius verò, cujus notitia ex priori sequitur, vel saltem eam excipit. Ordo naturæ vulgò statuitur vel naturæ generantis, vel naturæ intendentis: Ille ab imperfectioribus. Hic à perfectioribus incipit: ita quod primum est in intentione, ultimum est in executione: finis medijs prior est & perfectior. Talis etiam ordo intentionis pro nostro concipiendi modo statuitur in decretis divinis: ordo autem generationis conspicitur in eorundem executione: Deus, qui est author naturæ, est etiam author ordinis. Prius ergò naturâ dicitur id, sine quo alterum quod natura posterius est, esse vel intelligi nequit, etsi prius illud sine hoc posteriore esse vel intelligi queat: ita causa effectu, simplicia compositis, substantiæ accidentibus, subjecta adjunctis priora sunt.
units.tr: 77. The Order of Cognition is sought (1) from the nature of things: thus causes are prior to effects, and simples to composites, in knowledge; (2) from our own distinct and easy cognition: thus the mind is known before the body; (3) from common custom: thus sensible things are known before intellectual things. Therefore that is prior in cognition which is known before another; posterior is that whose knowledge follows from the prior, or at least presupposes it. The Order of Nature is commonly established either of generating nature or of intending nature. The former begins from the less perfect, the latter from the more perfect, so that what is first in intention is last in execution, and the end is prior to and more perfect than the means. Such an order of intention, according to our manner of conceiving, is established in the divine decrees; but the order of generation is seen in their execution. God, who is the author of nature, is also the author of order. That is prior by nature which is such that the other, which is posterior by nature, cannot be or be understood without it, although it can be or be understood without that posterior thing. Thus causes are prior to effects, simples to composites, substances to accidents, and subjects to adjuncts.

units.la: 78. Quemadmodum distinctio, ita & ordo inter personas SS. Trinitatis locum habet: sed quemadmodum distinctio illa plane est extraordinaria, ita & ordo
units.tr: 78. Just as the distinction holds among the persons of the Holy Trinity, so too does order; but just as that distinction is plainly extraordinary, so too the order

units.la: ordo hic plane extraordinarius est: ita ut si quæ prioritas ordinis hic locum habet, ea tantum quoad subsistendi & operandi ordinem sit intelligenda. Præcipuæ de Ordine regulæ Metaphysicorum sunt. In omni ordine persecto (ubi scilicet plura sunt quàm duo) datur primum, medium & ultimum: ac proinde in nullo ordine datur progressus in infinitum. 2. Medium non tantum distat ab extremis, quantum ipsa extrema inter se. 3. Subordinata non pugnant.
units.tr: order here is plainly extraordinary, so that if any priority of order has a place here, it is to be understood only with respect to the order of subsisting and of operating. The principal rules concerning Order are those of the Metaphysicians: (1) In every perfect order (namely where there are more than two terms) there is a first, a middle and a last, and therefore in no order is there progress to infinity; (2) The middle is not as far from the extremes as the extremes are from each other; (3) Subordinate things do not conflict.

units.la: 79. Post Relationem Originis & Negationis sequitur Relatio Affirmationis, qualis dicitur esse inter ea, quæ ita inter se consentiunt, ut tamen sine causalitatis vel dependentiæ ratione ad se invicem referantur. Quæ autem ad se invicem hac ratione referuntur, vel inter se comparantur, & vocatur Relatio Comparationis, unde hæc relata Comparata dicuntur: vel unum consideratur tanquam in alio, & vocatur Relatio Compositionis: vel unum spectatur tanquam accedens ad aliud, & vocatur Relatio Accessionis: vel deniq; unum ponitur pro alio & vocatur Relatio Substitutionis. Comparata sunt ea, quæ in aliquo tertio conveniunt, hoc autem tertium in quo conveniunt, vel quantitas est vel qualitas: Quæ in Quantitate conveniunt, Paria dicuntur sive æqualia. Quæ verò in Qualitate conveniunt, Similia vocantur. Convenientia quoad Substantiam non similitudinem, sed identitatem constituit: unde differentia inter ὁμοούσιον & ὁμοιούσιον.
units.tr: 79. After the Relation of Origin and of Negation follows the Relation of Affirmation, which is said to hold between things that agree with one another in such a way that they are nevertheless referred to one another without any ground of causality or dependence. Those things that are referred to one another, or compared with one another, in this way are said to have the Relation of Comparison, and so these related things are called compared. Or one thing is considered as being in another, and this is called the Relation of Composition. Or one thing is viewed as coming to another, and this is called the Relation of Accession. Or lastly, one thing is put in place of another, and this is called the Relation of Substitution. Things are compared when they agree in some third thing, and this third thing in which they agree is either quantity or quality. Things that agree in quantity are called equal or paria. Things that agree in quality are called similar. Agreement in substance constitutes not similarity but identity; hence the difference between ὁμοούσιον [homoousion] and ὁμοιούσιον [homoiousion].

units.la: 80. Relatio Compositionis est inter Compositum & inter ea, quæ compositum constituunt. Talis autem triplex esse videtur 1. vel inter Simplex & Compositum, 2. vel inter Totum & Partes. 3. vel inter Completum & Incompletum. Ita ergo vox Compositi aliquando latius sumitur, ut idem etiam sonet quod Totum vel Completum, imò Compositionem etiam ex Subjecto & Adjuncto, ex Substantia & Accidente, ex Genere & Differentia &c. complectatur: ita Simplex aliquando est, quod nullas habet partes: aliquando idem est, quod pars rei, aliquando res simplex neq; pars est neq; totum, quod partes habeat unde merus est vocabuli Totius abusus, cum terminus iste rei simplici tribuitur, e g. 1. Deo, cùm enim partes non habeat & simplicissimus sit, totus proprie non est appellandus. 2. Menti humanæ, cùm enim & hæc partes non habeat, nec partes ei sunt tribuendæ, nec tota est dicenda. Hinc veritas cognoscitur duarum regularum, quamvis in speciem videantur contrariæ. 1. Quò quid simplicius, eò perfectius. Vera est hæc regula de re, quæ partes non habet. e. g. de Deo, Mente, &c. 2. Composita sunt perfectiora simplicibus. Vera est regula de re, quæ ex partibus est composita, & omnes etiam partium perfectiones possidet.
units.tr: 80. The Relation of Composition holds between the composite and those things which constitute the composite. This relation seems to be threefold: (1) between simple and composite; (2) between whole and parts; (3) between complete and incomplete. So the word composite is sometimes taken more broadly, so that it means the same as whole or complete, and even embraces composition from subject and adjunct, from substance and accident, from genus and difference, and so on. Likewise simple sometimes means what has no parts; sometimes it means the same as a part of a thing; and sometimes a simple thing is neither a part nor a whole, since it has no parts. Hence the use of the word whole is simply a misuse when this term is applied to a simple thing: e.g. (1) to God, for since he has no parts and is most simple, he should not properly be called whole; (2) to the human mind, for since it too has no parts, parts should not be attributed to it, nor should it be called whole. From this the truth of two rules is recognized, although in appearance they seem contrary: (1) The simpler a thing is, the more perfect it is. This rule is true of a thing that has no parts, e.g. of God, mind, etc. (2) Composites are more perfect than simples. This rule is true of a thing that is composed of parts and also possesses all the perfections of its parts.

units.la: §1. Compositionem variè distinguunt Metaphysici: Nobis, cùm Distinctioni sic opposita, triplex quoque, ut ista, esse videtur, Realis, Modalis, & Rationis. Compositio Realis est ex partibus realiter distinctis: qualis est in homine ex mente & corpore, in corpore ex variis ejus partibus. Compositio Modalis est ex partibus, quarum una res est, alia modus rei, vel ex pluribus modis, e. g. ex Subjecto & Accidente, vel ex pluribus accidentibus. Compositio Rationis est ex attributis rei sola ratione inter se distinctis: qualis est e. g. ex essentia & existentia, ex actu & potentia, ex genere & differentia, quae Compositio alias Metaphysica vocatur.
units.tr: §1. The Metaphysicians distinguish composition in various ways. For us, since it is opposed to distinction in this way, it also seems to be threefold, as follows: real, modal, and of reason. Real composition is from parts really distinct: such as in man from mind and body, and in body from its various parts. Modal composition is from parts of which one is a thing and the other a mode of the thing, or from several modes, e.g. from subject and accident, or from several accidents. Composition of reason is from attributes of a thing that are distinguished from one another only by reason, such as from essence and existence, from act and potency, from genus and difference; this composition is otherwise called metaphysical.

units.la: Omnimodam Dei Simplicitatem negavit Vorstius, qui Attributa & Decreta Dei voluit esse accidentia, & proinde Deum ex essentia & accidentibus compositum statuit. Nos autem Deum Simplicissimum statuimus, in quem nec cadat I. Compositio Realis ex pluribus substantiis. II. Nec Modalis vel ex pluribus accidentibus vel ex substantia & accidentibus. Modi autem subsistendi in Deo plane sunt alterius generis, quibus similes non reperiuntur in tota rerum natura: ita ut si quae hic statuenda foret Compositio Distinctioni opposita, ea aeque ac haec plane extraordinaria foret. III. Nec Compositio Rationis 1 ex essentia & existentia, nam existentia est de essentia Dei. 2. ex potentia & actu, Deus enim est actus purifpurissimus. 3. ex genere & differentia, cùm enim singularissimus sit Deus, nec genus habet nec differentiam specisicam. 4. ex essentia & attributis: quamvis enim attributa Dei cùm ab essentia, cùm à se invicem ratione distinguantur, non tamen propterea Compositio Rationis in Deo est statuenda, cùm illa distinctio non tàm sit in Deo, quàm in nostra mente, atque fundamentum distinctionis potiùs sit extra Deum in diversis effectis & objectis, unde variæ ejusmodi relationes & denominationes externæ oriuntur.
units.tr: Vorstius denied the simplicity of God in every respect, holding that the attributes and decrees of God are accidents, and therefore affirming that God is composed of essence and accidents. We, however, hold that God is most simple, and in him there is neither (I) real composition from several substances, (II) nor modal composition, either from several accidents or from substance and accidents. For the modes of subsisting in God are plainly of another kind, and similar ones are not found in the whole of nature; so that if any composition opposed to distinction were to be posited here, it would be just as extraordinary as this distinction. (III) Nor is there composition of reason: (1) from essence and existence, for existence belongs to the essence of God; (2) from potency and act, for God is pure act; (3) from genus and difference, for since God is most singular, he has neither a genus nor a specific difference; (4) from essence and attributes. For although the attributes of God are distinguished both from the essence and from one another by reason, nevertheless a composition of reason should not therefore be posited in God, since this distinction is not so much in God as in our mind, and the ground of the distinction is rather outside God, in the diverse effects and objects, whence various such relations and external denominations arise.

units.la: §3. Totum est quod continet partes: estque vel Reale vel Notionale. Totum Reale est, quod partes habet revera distinctas: estque vel Essentiale vel Integrale. Totum Reale Essentiale est, in quo partes uniuntur ad constituendam essentiam: quales partes essentiales sunt Materia & Forma. Totum Reale Integrale est, cujus partes absolvunt materiam. Totum Notionale est, quod à nostro concipiendi modo dependet: estque vel Universale vel Essentiale le. Totum Notionale Universale est Genus, quod est totum suis inferioribus essentiale, de quo suo loco. Totum Notionale Essentiale est, quod constat genere & differentia: quale Totum vocatur Compositum Metaphysicum, cujus partes Metaphysicae sunt Genus & Differentia.
units.tr: §3. A whole is that which contains parts, and it is either real or notional. A real whole is that which has parts really distinct; and it is either essential or integral. A real essential whole is one in which the parts unite to constitute the essence; such essential parts are matter and form. A real integral whole is one whose parts complete the matter. A notional whole is one that depends on our mode of conceiving; and it is either universal or essential. A notional universal whole is a genus, which is a whole essential to its inferiors, concerning which see in its place. A notional essential whole is one that consists of genus and difference; such a whole is called a metaphysical composite, whose metaphysical parts are genus and difference.

units.la: Pars est vel Essentialis vel Integralis. Pars Essentialis est vel Metaphysica vel Physica. Pars Integralis est vel Principalis vel Minus Principalis. Pars etiam alia est Homogenea, alia Heterogenea: nec etiam omne quod est in corpore, ejus pars est: sicut enim mali humores non sunt membra corporis humani, ita nec mali proprie membra sunt Ecclesiae. Tota res dicitur de eo quod compositum est & suas habet partes; sed Totum rei dicuntur omnes & singulae ejus partes, sive conjunctim sive seorsim sumptae: ita e. g. totus Christus est ubique, sed non totum Christi: scilicet non secundum naturam humanam. Christus pro nobis mortuus est, sed non totum Christi, non enim mortuus est secundum divinam naturam.
units.tr: A part is either essential or integral. An essential part is either metaphysical or physical. An integral part is either principal or less principal. A part is also one thing homogeneous and another heterogeneous; nor is everything that is in a body a part of it: for just as bad humours are not members of the human body, so bad people are not properly members of the Church. A thing as a whole is said of that which is composite and has its own parts; but the whole of a thing is said of all and each of its parts, whether taken together or separately. Thus, e.g., whole Christ is everywhere, but not the whole of Christ, namely not according to his human nature. Christ died for us, but not the whole of Christ, for he did not die according to his divine nature.

units.la: 8§. Ens Completum ad Incompletum aliquando se habet ut Totum ad Partem: ita enim Totum est Ens Completum, Pars vero est Ens Incompletum. Interim tamen 1. Non omne Completum partes habet, Deus enim est Ens Completum, & tamen partes non habet. 2. Quae Pars est, potest esse Ens Completum, si à nobis non consideretur ut pars alterius rei. E. G. Mens humana, quamvis sit pars hominis, à corpore tamen separata non incompletum, sed completum est ens: ut non absurdè Mentem à Corpore separatam Suppositum vel Persona nonnulli vocent: ita enim una eademque res potest esse suppositum & non esse, prout nempè vel ut per se vel ut pars alterius rei consideratur: Sed aliquando Suppositi nomen tribuitur toti composito, quo sensu vulgò dicunt, Actiones esse Suppositorum. E. G. Quamvis in Christo Θεανθρώπω duplex sit substantia, divina & humana, actiones tamen supposito h. e. toti personae adscribuntur.
units.tr: §8. A complete being is sometimes related to an incomplete being as a whole to a part: for thus the whole is a complete being, and the part is an incomplete being. Nevertheless: (1) Not every complete thing has parts, for God is a complete being, and yet has no parts. (2) What is a part can be a complete being, if it is not considered by us as a part of another thing. E.g. the human mind, although it is a part of man, is nevertheless, when separated from the body, not an incomplete but a complete being; so that some not absurdly call the mind separated from the body a suppositum or person; for one and the same thing can be a suppositum and not be one, according as it is considered either as existing in itself or as a part of another thing. But sometimes the name of suppositum is given to the whole composite, in which sense people commonly say actions belong to supposita. E.g. although in Christ the God-man there are two substances, divine and human, actions are nevertheless ascribed to the suppositum, i.e. to the whole person.

units.la: In Abstractis & Concretis Simplicitas & Compositio tantùm est pro nostro concipiendi modo. Ea enim, quæ simplicissima sunt in conceptu nostro, Abstracta dicuntur. Quæ verò minùs simplicia sunt, vel ubi plura simul conceptui nostro objiciuntur, Concreta vocantur. Abstrahere enim in Philosophia est rem unam sine alia considerare. Attributa de Deo non in Concreto tantùm, sed in Abstracto quoque prædicari possunt, e.g. Deus non tantùm est sapiens, sed ipsa sapientia; Nam attributa ab essentia non differunt, & proinde vocabula Concreta, quæ de Deo usurpantur, non notant aliquid compositum vel concretum in Deo, sed omnem compositionem à nostro tantùm concipiendi modo ortam ostendunt.
units.tr: In abstract and concrete terms, simplicity and composition are only a matter of our way of conceiving. Those things that are most simple in our concept are called abstract. Those that are less simple, or where several things are presented to our concept at once, are called concrete. For in philosophy to abstract means to consider one thing without another. Attributes of God can be predicated not only in the concrete but also in the abstract, e.g. God is not only wise but wisdom itself. For the attributes do not differ from the essence, and so the concrete terms used of God do not signify anything composite or concrete in God, but show only that all composition arises from our manner of conceiving.

units.la: Relatio Accessionis est ea, quæ est inter Subjectum & ejus Adjunctum: Hoc enim ad Subjectum accedit. Subjectum hic latissimo sensu est Ens, cui aliquid præter essentiam accedit, ita ut hoc sensu non tantùm Substantia, sed & Acci& Accidens sua habeat Adjuncta. AdjuncVum est id, quod Subjecto præter essentiam accedit: h. e, quod ad essentiam ita accedit, ut neque eam constituat, neque eam necessario consequatur, sive jam res sit sive modus rei. Attributum latius patet quàm Adjunctum, cùm illud Subjecto aliquando essentiale, hoc verò accidentale tantùm existat: quamvis Ramus in Logica Proprietates etiam ad Adjuncta referat. Subjectum est vel Recipiens vel Occupans. Illud Subjecti nomen retinet, hoc Objectum vocatur, unde frequentissima in Scholis Subjectivi & Objectivi distinctio. Subjectum etiam aliud est Inhasionis, aliud Denominationis: In Disciplinis Subjectum aliud est Informationis, aliud Tractationis, quod cum Objecto coincidit. Hoc autem Objectum est vel Materiale, hoc est, res quæ consideratur, vel Formale, h. e. considerandi modus: Aliud etiam est Adæquatum, aliud Inadæquatum, aliud Principale & aliud Minus Principale.
units.tr: The relation of accession is that which holds between a subject and its adjunct, for the adjunct accedes to the subject. Here subject is taken in the widest sense as any being to which something accedes besides its essence, so that in this sense not only a substance but also an accident may have its own adjuncts. An adjunct is that which accedes to a subject besides its essence: that is, it accedes to the essence in such a way that it neither constitutes it nor necessarily follows from it, whether it be a thing or a mode of a thing. An attribute has a wider range than an adjunct, since the former may sometimes exist essentially in its subject, whereas the latter exists only accidentally, although Ramus in his Logic also refers properties to adjuncts. A subject is either receiving or occupying. The former keeps the name subject, the latter is called the object, whence the very frequent distinction in the schools between subjective and objective. A subject is also one thing with respect to inherence and another with respect to denomination. In the disciplines, the subject is one thing with respect to information and another with respect to treatment, which coincides with the object. This object is either material, that is, the thing considered, or formal, that is, the mode of considering. There is also one kind that is adequate and another that is inadequate, one that is principal and another that is less principal.

units.la: 88. Præcipua de Subjecto & Adjuncto A- xiomata
units.tr: 88. The Principal Axioms concerning Subject and Adjunct

units.la: xiomata sunt 1 Unius rei sive Subjecti plura possunt esse Adjuncta: Unius etiam Adjuncti plura possunt esse alia Adjuncta: sed ita tamen, ut haec omnia tandem & ultimo in uno aliquo Subjecto conveniant, quod ideo ut Principale spectatur, cum reliqua conside rentur ut Accessoria: ita enim quod Accessorium est, primarij est Adjunctum.
units.tr: The axioms are: 1. One subject can have several adjuncts; and one adjunct can also have several other adjuncts; but in such a way that all of these finally and ultimately agree in some one subject, which is therefore regarded as principal, while the rest are considered as accessory; for what is accessory is an adjunct of the principal.

units.la: Quando autem plura sunt Adjuncta, non difficile est determinare, utrum eorum Subjectum sit aut Adjunctum, nam plerumque hoc determinandum est vel ex magnitudine vel ex toto, cujus parti tantummodo aliquid accedit, vel ex aliquo alio respectu: ita magnitudinem gladij longioris respexit Cicero, quando generum suum ad gladium alligatum dixit: ita Chirotheca adjunctum manus censetur, quia totus homo gestare chirothecam dicitur, quamvis parti tantum, manui scilicet applicetur &c. Uno verbo: Quod Accessorium est & a nobis ut tale consideratur, id Adjunctum potius est quam Subjectum.
units.tr: When, however, there are several adjuncts, it is not difficult to determine which of them is the subject and which the adjunct; for this is usually to be determined either from magnitude, or from the whole of which something accedes only to a part, or from some other respect. Thus Cicero had regard to the size of a longer sword when he said that his kinsman was tied to a sword; thus a glove is judged to be an adjunct of the hand, because a whole man is said to wear a glove, although it is applied only to a part, namely the hand, etc. In a word: whatever is accessory and is regarded by us as such, is rather an adjunct than a subject.

units.la: 2. Adjunctum non potest latius patere re suo Subjecto. Quemadmodum enim Accidens non potest esse sine Substantia, ita nec Adjunctum potest esse sine Subjecto: At vero si Adjunctum latius pateret suo Subjecto, eatenus illud esset extra Subjectum, & ita sine Subjecto. Imò hac ratione quod Accessorium est, fieret Principale, & tamen esset Accessorium, quod implicat.
units.tr: 2. An adjunct cannot extend more widely than its own subject. For just as an accident cannot exist without a substance, so an adjunct cannot exist without a subject. But if the adjunct extended more widely than its subject, then to that extent it would be outside the subject, and so without a subject. Indeed, in this way what is accessory would become principal, and yet would remain accessory, which is contradictory.

units.la: 3. Finitum non est capax infiniti. Alias Adjunctum esset extra Subjectum, eoque latius pateret: Hinc sobrie nobis, qui finiti sumus de infinito philosophandum, nec facile rei, quae finita est, infinitum quid tribuendum.
units.tr: 3. What is finite is not capable of the infinite. Otherwise the adjunct would be outside the subject and would extend more widely than it. Hence we who are finite must philosophise soberly about the infinite, and we must not easily ascribe to a finite thing anything infinite.

units.la: 4. Adjunctum sequitur suum Subjectum, Accessorium suum Principale. H. e. Quale est Subjectum, tale etiam est Adjunctum: ita enim quod est Subjectum Corporeum, non potest habere Adjuncta Spiritualia, & quod est Subjectum Spirituale, non potest habere Adjuncta Corporea: quod Subjectum est finitum, non potest habere Adjuncta infinita, & quod est Subjectum creatum, non potest habere Adjuncta increata: unde Axioma Logicum: Talia sunt prædicata, qualia permittuntur esse à suis subjectis. 5. Sublato Subjecto tollitur quoque Adjunctum, sed non vice versa: quia unius Subjecti plura possunt esse Adjuncta, uno ergo sublato non statim Subjectum tollitur: Sed nullum est Adjunctum, quod non suum habeat Subjectum: quod in specie observandum est de Accidentibus, quæ extra Subjectum vel sine Subjecto existere nequeunt.
units.tr: 4. An adjunct follows its subject, and an accessory its principal. That is, whatever kind of subject it is, such also is its adjunct. Thus what is a corporeal subject cannot have spiritual adjuncts, and what is a spiritual subject cannot have corporeal adjuncts; what is a finite subject cannot have infinite adjuncts, and what is a created subject cannot have uncreated adjuncts. Hence the logical axiom: Predicates are such as their subjects permit them to be. 5. When the subject is removed, the adjunct is removed too, but not vice versa, because one subject can have several adjuncts, so that on the removal of one the subject is not immediately removed. But there is no adjunct that does not have its own subject; this is to be observed especially of accidents, which cannot exist outside a subject or without a subject.

units.la: 91. Relatio Substitutionis est qua unum ponitur pro alio, estq; triplex: vel inter Signum & Signatum, vel inter Mensuram & Mensuratum, vel inter Imaginem & Exemplar. Relationem autem inter Signum & Signatum ideo præmittimus, quia & Mensura est signum Quantitatem indicans, & Imago est signum sui exemplaris. Signum alii definiunt ens, quod potentia cognoscenti aliquid occultum repræsentat: Verùm quia non omne signum repræsentat, alij Signum definire malunt, quod semet ipsum sensibus, & id cujus est signum intellectui offert. Verùm cùm & bruta, quæ intellectu destituta sunt, & mentes vel angelicæ vel humanæ à corpore separatæ, quæ sensus non habent, signis uti videantur, nobis adhuc generaliùs Signum definiendum videtur per id, quod aliquid à se distinctum notum facit, sive id duntaxat indicet sive insuper repræsentet; undè Signum in Instrumentale & Formale distinguitur.
units.tr: 91. The relation of substitution is that by which one thing is put in place of another, and it is threefold: either between sign and signified, or between measure and measured, or between image and exemplar. We put the relation between sign and signified first, because a measure is also a sign indicating quantity, and an image is a sign of its exemplar. Some define a sign as a being which, by its power, represents something hidden to one who knows. But since not every sign represents, others prefer to define a sign as that which offers itself to the senses and offers to the intellect that of which it is a sign. But since both brute animals, which lack intellect, and angelic or human minds separated from the body, which have no senses, seem to make use of signs, it seems to us that a sign must be defined more generally as that which makes known something distinct from itself, whether it merely indicates or moreover represents it; hence a sign is distinguished into instrumental and formal.

units.la: Signum Instrumentale est, quod rem tantùm indicat, non verò repræsentat: ut fumus ignem, hedera vinum vendibile; ita ut præter speciem, quam primo intuitu menti ingerit, aliud aliquid menti cognoscendum præbeat, e. g. panis in S. Cæna: vocatur etiam Signum Materiale. Signum Formale est, quod rem non tantùm indicat, sed etiam repræsentat: qualia signa sunt rerum imagines: ita autem res à mente distinctæ, & per ejusmodi signa menti repræsentatæ proprie non sunt in mente nisi objectivè, nam quoad esse proprium manent extra mentem & à mente distincta sunt entia. Aliâs in ipso quoqÿ
units.tr: An instrumental sign is that which merely indicates a thing and does not represent it, as smoke indicates fire, or ivy indicates wine for sale; so that, besides the species which it first impresses on the mind at a glance, it offers something else to be known by the mind, as for instance the bread in the Lord's Supper. It is also called a material sign. A formal sign is that which not only indicates a thing but also represents it, such as images of things are. Things distinct from the mind, and represented to the mind through such signs, are properly in the mind only objectively, for with respect to their own being they remain outside the mind and are beings distinct from the mind. Otherwise, in the very ...

units.la: Signo Materiale & Formale distinguitur: Signi Materiale est ejus esse proprium, quod res extra mentem cognoscentem habet. Vocatur etiam ejus Esse Reale. Sed Formale Signi est ejus esse vicarium in mente cognoscentis, vel est relatio ad rem occultam significandam. Vocatur etiam ejus Esse Intentionale & Objectivum: ita Sacramenta materialiter sunt res naturales, formaliter sunt signa. Voces materialiter sumuntur pro literis & syllabis, formaliter pro rebus significatis. Hoc sensu sumitur nomen Jesu Phil. 2:10.
units.tr: A sign is distinguished into material and formal. The material of a sign is its own being, which it has outside the knowing mind; this is also called its real being. But the formal of a sign is its vicarious being in the mind of the knower, or it is its relation to the hidden thing to be signified. It is also called its intentional and objective being. Thus sacraments are materially natural things, but formally they are signs. Words are taken materially for letters and syllables, but formally for the things signified. In this sense the name of Jesus is taken in Phil. 2:10.

units.la: Hinc patet 1. Quomodò duplex realitas in Signo duplicem posset habere causam: aliam nempe secundum esse proprium & materiale, aliam secundum esse vicarium: ita Idea Dei aliam habet causam, quando ut cogitandi modus vel ut mentis operatio spectatur; aliam cum spectatur ut imago Deum repræsentans. 2. Quomodò quis possit esse particeps signi, ut tamen non sit particeps rei signata. Propter relationem autem inter Signum & Signatum, (sive id, quod per signum indicatur & repræsentatur) sæpè fit, ut Signum rei signata & res signata signi nomine indigitetur: qualis loquendi modus frequentissimus in Sacramentis, unde etiam Tropus Sacramentalis vocatur.
units.tr: From this it is clear, first, how a twofold reality in a sign could have a twofold cause: one, namely according to its proper and material being, and another according to its vicarious being. Thus the idea of God has one cause when it is considered as a mode of thinking or an operation of the mind, and another when it is considered as an image representing God. Second, how someone can be a participant in a sign without being a participant in the thing signified. On account of the relation between sign and signified (that is, that which is indicated and represented through the sign), it often happens that the sign is named by the name of the thing signified, and the thing signified by the name of the sign; this manner of speaking is most frequent in the sacraments, whence it is also called the sacramental trope.

units.la: Quæritur hîc 1. Quomodò Angelis & mentibus à Corpore separatis tribuenda sit cognitio per signa? 2. Quomodò Menti humanæ cum corpore conjunctæ, 3. Quomodò Brutis? R. ad I. Quicquid spiritus cognoscunt, illud cognoscunt per eas, quas de rebus habent ideas: sed cùm inter ideas ipsas, & inter ideas etiam & res exteriores certus sit nexus, quo vel naturaliter vel ex compacto vel pro intelligentis arbitrio sunt connexæ, hinc fit, ut quoties res aliqua externa se offert, propter nexum à Deo institutum idea excitetur in mente & cum hac alia etiam idea, quæ cum ea est connexa, & ita res illa, quæ facit, ut mens priorem eliciat ideam, potest esse signum rei illius, quam posterior idea repræsentat. E. G. Angelo Destructorî Ætori Sanguis Aspersus signum erat non occidendorum primogenitorum, quia Deus voluit esse nexum inter ideam sanguinis aspersi & inter transitum faciendum ab angelo: & ita res illa, quæ occasio erat excitandæ prioris ideæ signum erat posterioris.
units.tr: The question here is: 1. How is knowledge through signs to be attributed to angels and minds separated from the body? 2. How to the human mind joined with the body? 3. How to brutes? Answer to 1: Whatever spirits know, they know through the ideas they have of things. Since there is a certain connection among the ideas themselves, and between ideas and external things, by which they are linked either naturally, or by agreement, or by the will of the intelligent being, it follows that whenever some external thing presents itself, an idea is aroused in the mind by the connection God has instituted, and with it another idea connected to it. So that thing which causes the mind to produce the first idea can be a sign of the thing the second idea represents. For example, for the destroying angel the sprinkled blood was a sign that the firstborn were not to be killed, because God willed a connection between the idea of the sprinkled blood and the passing over to be made by the angel. Thus the thing which was the occasion for arousing the first idea was a sign of the second.

units.la: 95. Ad 2. ℟. α. Variæ fiunt in cerebro impressiones mediante nervorum & spirituum animalium motu. β. Hic impressionibus naturaliter connexæ sunt certæ ideæ. γ. Impressiones illæ certum inter se nexum habent sive naturalem sive proprio arbitrio ac frequentiore consuetudine firmatum. δ. Et quia cum singulis illis in cerebro impressionibus singulæ etiam conjunctæ sunt in mente nostra ideæ, hinc fit, ut quamprimum nobis res aliqua obversatur, quæ priorem impressionem excitare apta est, utraque statim impressio excitetur, & proinde utriusque etiam idea: Ita Res illa, quæ occasionem præbet cerebro priorem impressionem recipiendi, dum nervos & spiritus animales certo modo movet, posterioris Signum vocatur. Ad 3. ℞. Eo modo, quo Sensus Brutis attribui potest, in quibus primus tantum sentiendi gradus locum habet, nec enim aliter Signa Brutis sunt tribuenda, quàm quatenus cum una cerebri impressione connexa est & alia: E. G. cùm Canis baculum videt, non ea tantùm in cerebro fit impressio, quæ necessaria est ad videndum baculum, sed cum ea impressione conjuncta est & alia in cerebro impressio, talis nempè qualis tunc erat, quando baculo canis percussus fuit, undè Baculus in posterum cani Signum est accipiendorum verberum.
units.tr: 95. To 2. Answer: α. Various impressions are made in the brain through the motion of the nerves and animal spirits. β. Certain ideas are naturally connected with these impressions. γ. These impressions have a certain connection among themselves, whether natural, or established by their own choice and more frequent custom. δ. And because with each of those impressions in the brain, each of the ideas is also joined in our mind, it follows that as soon as some thing presents itself to us which is apt to excite the former impression, both impressions are immediately excited, and so too both ideas. Thus that thing which gives the brain the occasion of receiving the former impression, while it moves the nerves and animal spirits in a certain way, is called a sign of the latter. To 3. Answer: In the way in which sense can be attributed to brutes, in whom only the first degree of sensing takes place. Signs are not to be attributed to brutes otherwise than insofar as one impression in the brain is connected with another. For example, when a dog sees a stick, there is produced in the brain not only the impression necessary for seeing the stick, but another impression is joined to it in the brain, namely such as was there when the dog was struck with a stick. Hence the stick becomes a sign to the dog in future of blows to be received.

units.la: Signum variè distinguitur à Metaphysicis, nam I. vel Naturale est vel Arbitrarium. Naturale est, quod naturâ suâ aliquid significat: Dicitur Signum per se, quia periculum est ex ipsa rei natura, unde qui rei naturam novit, talè etiam signum statim cognoscit, e. g. fumus respectu ignis. Est autem hoc Signum Naturale vel Antecedens, & est causa vel necessarium antecedens respectu eventus venturi: vel Concomitans, & est essectum respectu causæ coexistentis vel respectu effecti socij, quod simul est tempore & ab eadem causa procedit: vel Consequens, & est effectum respectu causæ præcedentis vel aliud aliquod consequens necessarium. Signum Arbitrarium five ex inftitucto tale est, quod ex institutione vel divina vel humana aliquid significati ita e. g. hedera signum est vini vendibilis, Sacramentum gratiæ conserendæ: ita nomina sunt signa rerum, quamvis enim homini naturale sit loqui & signis quibusdam alligare suas cogitationes, est tamen ab hominum arbitrio, quod his potius quàm alijs vocabulis has potius quàm alias cogitationes designent, aliâs omnes homines ijsdem vocibus easdem ideas exprimerent. Idem Signum potest effe & naturale & arbitrarium, sed diverso respectu, e. g. Iris: ita typi rerum futurarum sunt signa arbitraria, sed sunt signa quodammodo naturalia, prout inter typum & rem typo signisignificatam convenientia intercedit: ita Sacramenta &c.
units.tr: Metaphysicians distinguish a sign in various ways. I. It is either natural or arbitrary. A natural sign is that which signifies something by its nature. It is called a sign per se, because the connection arises from the very nature of the thing, so that whoever knows the nature of the thing at once recognises such a sign, e.g. smoke with respect to fire. This natural sign is either antecedent, and is a cause or a necessary antecedent with respect to a future event; or concomitant, and is an effect with respect to a coexisting cause, or with respect to a companion effect which is simultaneous in time and proceeds from the same cause; or consequent, and is an effect with respect to a preceding cause or some other necessary consequent. An arbitrary sign, that is, one by institution, is that which signifies something by institution, either divine or human: thus e.g. the ivy bush is a sign of saleable wine, and a sacrament is a sign of grace to be conferred. So words are signs of things. For although it is natural for man to speak and to bind his thoughts to certain signs, it is by the will of men that these words rather than others designate these thoughts rather than others; otherwise all men would express the same ideas by the same words. The same sign can be both natural and arbitrary, but with a different respect: e.g. the rainbow. Thus types of future things are arbitrary signs, but are in a certain way natural signs, insofar as a fitting relation lies between the type and the thing signified by the type. So too sacraments, etc.

units.la: II.Signum est vel Necessarium vel Contingens. Necessarium (Græcè Τεκμήριον) vocatur, quod infallibiliter rem aliquam significat: ita e. g. ex Miraculis tanquam ex signo necessario Christus verus Deus & Mundi Messias probatur. Signum Contingens vocatur, quod probabiliter tantùm aliquid notificat: qualia signa ἐνδότα Græcè dicuntur: e. g. rubedo cœli matutina signum est futuræ pluviæ. III Signum est vel Theoreticum vel Practicum. Theoreticum sive Speculativum vocatur, quod rem signatam simpliciter significat vel repræsentat. Signum autem Practicum vocatur illud, quod simul rei signatæ exhibitivum est, e. g. pignus, sigillum, arrha, sacramenta &c. unde & Signa Certificantia dicuntur.
units.tr: II. A sign is either necessary or contingent. What infallibly signifies some thing is called necessary (in Greek tekmērion [Τεκμήριον]): thus, e.g., from miracles, as from a necessary sign, Christ is proved to be true God and the Messiah of the world. What only probably makes something known is called a contingent sign; such signs are called endota [ἐνδότα] in Greek: e.g. the reddening of the sky in the morning is a sign of future rain. III. A sign is either theoretical or practical. What simply signifies or represents the thing signified is called theoretical or speculative. That which at the same time exhibits the thing signified is called a practical sign, e.g. a pledge, a seal, an earnest, sacraments, etc., whence they are also called assuring signs.

units.la: IV. Signum est vel Memoriale vel Prognosticum vel Demonstrativum. Memoriale (vel Commemorativum) est, quod conservat rei præteritæ memoriam, e. g. cicatrix vulneris. Prognosticum est signum rei futurae, e. g. typi Veteris Testamenti. Demonstrativum sive Diagnosticum est, quod praesens demonstrat: ita e. g. Iris pluviae & respiratio vitae signum est. Sed Panis & Vinum in S. Coena signa sunt commemorativa, & proinde rei praeteritae, non praesentis, ut vellent Pontificij.
units.tr: IV. A sign is either memorial, prognostic or demonstrative. A memorial (or commemorative) sign is what preserves the memory of a past thing, e.g. the scar of a wound. A prognostic sign is a sign of a future thing, e.g. the types of the Old Testament. A demonstrative or diagnostic sign is what demonstrates the present: thus e.g. the rainbow is a sign of rain, and breathing a sign of life. But bread and wine in the Holy Supper are commemorative signs, and so of a past thing, not a present one, as the Papists would have it.

units.la: Ad Signum etiam Mensura pertinet: Mensura enim est signum quod notificat quantitatem, sive perfectionis, sive extensionis, sive intensionis, sive successionis, sive multitudinis: unde Mensura etiam vel Perfectionis vel Extensionis vel Intensionis vel Successionis vel Multitudinis vocatur: alij etiam Mensuram Cognitionis addunt. Mensuratum vero vocatur id omne, quod quocunq; horum modorum mensuratur. Mensura perfectionis est id, quod perfectissimum est in unoquoq; genere: sive est regula ac norma, juxta quam de rei alicujus perfectione judicamus: ita Deus est mensura omnis perfectionis, Lex Dei Legum humanarum, Vita Christi vitae nostrae: ita Idea rei dici sic ci solet mensura rerum, quia res in abstracto considerata consideratur in idea sua, idea enim rei formatur juxta definitionem, res autem definienda est in suo perfectissimo gradu, ut ab ea omnis imperfectio abstrahatur. Mensura Extensionis est ea, ad quam mensuratur magnitudo corporis, h. e. quantitas extensionis, quæ uno nomine magnitudo vocatur, cujus partes sunt longitudo, latitudo & profunditas: ita ulna, pes, &c. mensuræ sunt, quibus vel lineæ alicujus longitudo vel superficiei magnitudo, vel corporis solidi capacitas mensuratur. Hanc alij Applicationis Mensuram vocant, & ad eam quoque Ponderis mensuram revocant.
units.tr: Measure also belongs to the category of sign, for a measure is a sign that makes known a quantity, whether of perfection, extension, intension, succession, or multitude. Hence measure is also called measure of perfection, of extension, of intension, of succession, or of multitude; others also add measure of cognition. Whatever is measured by any of these modes is called the measured. Measure of perfection is that which is most perfect in each genus; or it is the rule and norm by which we judge the perfection of some thing. Thus God is the measure of all perfection, God's law the measure of human laws, Christ's life the measure of our life. So too the idea of a thing is customarily called the measure of things, because a thing considered in the abstract is considered in its idea: the idea of a thing is formed according to its definition, and the thing to be defined must be taken in its most perfect degree, so that all imperfection is abstracted from it. Measure of extension is that by which the magnitude of a body is measured, that is, the quantity of extension, which by one name is called magnitude, and whose parts are length, breadth and depth. Thus the ell, the foot, etc. are measures by which the length of some line, the magnitude of a surface, or the capacity of a solid body is measured. Others call this the measure of application, and they also refer the measure of weight to it.

units.la: Mensura Intensionis est ea, qua qualitatis gradus à nobis cognoscuntur: e.g. calor manus est mensura caloris in aqua: huc ergo varia graduum mensura pertinet. Mensura Successionis est ea, qua rerum durationem mensurare solemus, ut sunt 1. Motus Cælorum, Solis, Lunæ, &c. 2. Motus particularis alicujus corporis, ut Horologij, arenæ in clepsammio, &c. Ad ejusmodi autem mensuram non tantum mensurare licet durationem motus & quietis in corporibus, sed durationem etiam spirituum variarumque cogitationum sibi succedentium : Mensura multitudinis est ea, qua rerum multitudo vel numerus mensuratur ; vocatur etiam Mensura repetitionis: ita unitas est mensura numeri, quia unicas aliquoties repetita talem vel talem numerum efficit. Mensura Cognitionis vocatur ea, ad cujus normam aliquid cognoscimus, unde & Cognoscendi norma vocatur: qualis est e. g. Sacra Scriptura ratione Theologiae. Tria autem sunt Mensurae requisita. 1. Ut sit homogenea mensurando: male ergo Philosophia statuitur norma interpretandi Sacram Scripturam. 2. Ut sit certa & fixa. Errant ergo, qui sensus volunt esse principium & normam in Philosophia; vel qui Patrum & Conciliorum Decreta statuunt religionis normam. 3. Ut sit notior mensurando: unde male Pontificij S. Scripturam obscuritatis arguunt.
units.tr: Measure of intension is that by which we know the degrees of a quality: e.g. the warmth of the hand is a measure of the heat in water. To this therefore belongs the various measure of degrees. Measure of succession is that by which we are accustomed to measure the duration of things, such as 1. the motions of the heavens, the sun, the moon, etc.; 2. the particular motion of some body, such as a clock, or sand in an hourglass, etc. By such a measure it is permitted to measure not only the duration of motion and rest in bodies, but also the duration of spirits and of various thoughts succeeding one another. Measure of multitude is that by which the multitude or number of things is measured; it is also called measure of repetition. Thus unity is the measure of number, because a unit repeated a certain number of times makes such and such a number. Measure of cognition is that by whose norm we know something, whence it is also called the norm of knowing: such is, e.g., Holy Scripture with respect to theology. Three things are required of a measure. 1. That it be homogeneous with what is measured: wrongly, then, is philosophy set up as the norm for interpreting Holy Scripture. 2. That it be certain and fixed. Those err, therefore, who want the senses to be the principle and norm in philosophy, or who set up the decrees of the Fathers and Councils as the norm of religion. 3. That it be better known than what is measured: whence the Papists wrongly accuse Holy Scripture of obscurity.

units.la: 100. Quemadmodum Exemplar Signati ita Imago quoque Signi rationem habet. Exemplar est id, unde aliquid per imitationem expressum est. Imago vero est quicquid ad aliud per imitationem expressum est. Alias etiam Exemplar Archetypum, Imago vero Ectypum vocatur. Exemplar scriptum Autographum, & quod inde descriptum est, Apographum dicitur. Non quaelibet similitudo Imaginem facit, unde quamvis ubique in creaturis conspicua sint sapientiæ, bonitatis ac potentiæ divinæ vestigia, non tamen omnes creaturæ ad Imaginem Dei creatæ dicuntur, sed solæ creaturæ rationales, imò disputatur adhuc in Scholis, in quo præcisè imago illa Dei consistat? & an eadem etiam post peccatum in natura rationali locum habeat? Præcipua de Imagine regula hæc est: Non potest esse plus perfectionis in imagine quàm reperitur in ejus exemplari vel in eo, quod exemplaris vicem sustinet: ita enim exemplar ad locum de Causa, imago vero ad Effectum pertinet; jam vero nihil est in Effectu quod non sit in Causa vel formaliter vel eminenter.
units.tr: 100. Just as an exemplar has the character of a sign, so too does an image. The exemplar is that from which something is expressed by imitation; an image is whatever is expressed by imitation after something else. Sometimes the exemplar is also called the archetype, and the image the ectype. A written exemplar is called the autograph, and what has been copied from it is called the apograph. Not every likeness makes an image. Hence, although traces of divine wisdom, goodness and power are visible everywhere in creatures, not all creatures are said to be created "in the image of God", but only rational creatures. Indeed, it is still disputed in the Schools precisely in what that image of God consists, and whether it remains in rational nature after the fall. The chief rule concerning the image is this: there can be no more perfection in the image than is found in its exemplar, or in that which takes the place of the exemplar. For the exemplar belongs to the category of cause, and the image to that of effect; now there is nothing in an effect that is not in its cause, either formally or eminently.

units.la: 101. Ad hanc doctrinam etiam pertinet Doctrina de Ideis sive Divinis sive Hu- manis.
units.tr: 101. To this doctrine also belongs the doctrine of Ideas, both divine and human.

units.la: Idea divina sunt rerum creatarum exemplaria: Idea vero Humana sunt rerum imagines. De his audiamus Amesium Med Theol. cap. 7.
units.tr: Divine ideas are the exemplars of created things, but human ideas are the images of things. On these, let us hear Amesius, Med. Theol. ch. 7.

units.la: Idea in homine, qui cognitionem acquirit per Analysin, colligitur ex rebus ipsis: atq; adeo res primò in semetipsis existunt, tum ad hominum sensum perveniunt, & inde ad intellectum, ubi possunt ideam aliquam constituere ad operationem insequentem dirigendam. Sed quoniam Deus intelligit omnia per genesin, & non requirit cognitionem per analysin rerum, ideò omnia sunt prius in ejus mente, quàm in semet ipsis. In nobis res ipsæ sunt exemplar, & cognitio nostra est imago. Sed in Deo scientia divina est exemplar, & res ipsæ sunt imago vel similitudo ejus expressa. Idea in homine est prius impressa, & postea exprimitur in rebus: sed in Deo est tantùm exprimens proprie, non impressa, quia non accedit aliundè.
units.tr: An idea in a human being, who acquires knowledge by analysis, is gathered from the things themselves. Thus things first exist in themselves, then come to the sense of men, and from there to the intellect, where they can form some idea to direct the action that follows. But since God understands all things by genesis, and does not need knowledge of things by analysis, all things are therefore first in his mind, before they are in themselves. In us the things themselves are the exemplar, and our knowledge is the image. But in God the divine knowledge is the exemplar, and the things themselves are the image or expressed likeness of it. In a human being the idea is first impressed, and afterwards expressed in things; but in God it is only expressing, properly speaking, not impressed, because it comes from nowhere else.

units.la: 102. Idea Dei nihil aliud est quàm scientia in Deo, secundùm quam Deus ab æterno ex decreto voluntatis suæ scivit, quid facturus esset, & quomodo facturus esset unamquamque rem secundum circumstantias ejus & momenta: ita ut hac ratione Idea Dei sit exemplar & archetypon omnium rerum producendarum, quae sunt totidem illius ideae imagines: & hoc modo etiam explicandae videntur Ideae Platonicae. Ideae autem nostrae non sunt exemplaria, sed sunt imagines rerum cogitatarum; unde hae etiam quatenus tales causam aliquam requirunt, in qua tantundem perfectionis vel formaliter vel eminenter contineatur, quantum perfectionis objectivae continetur in ipsis ideis; juxta regulem: Realitas Objectiva cujuslibet ideae requirit causam exemplarem vel quae causa exemplaris vicem sustineat, in qua persectio illa formaliter vel eminenter contineatur. Una imago potest quidem esse causa alterius imaginis, & haec iterum alterius, sed tandem tamen deveniendum est ad primum aliquod exemplar, & in eo subsistendum, nec enim progressus in infinitum hic dari potest. Haec autem de Causa exemplari cujuslibet idea regula insignem in Philosophia usum habet: nam fundamentum est 1. demonstrationis illius, qua ex idea Dei pro ejus existentia argumentamur. 2. omnis illius certitudinis, quam ex sensibus habemus.
units.tr: 102. The idea of God is nothing other than knowledge in God, according to which God, from eternity, by the decree of his will, knew what he would make, and how he would make each thing according to its circumstances and details. So in this way the idea of God is the exemplar and archetype of all things to be produced, which are so many images of that idea; and in this way Platonic Ideas also seem to be explained. Our ideas, however, are not exemplars, but are images of things thought of. Hence these also, insofar as they are such, require some cause in which just as much perfection is contained, either formally or eminently, as the objective perfection contained in the ideas themselves; according to the rule: The objective reality of any idea requires an exemplar cause, or a cause that takes the place of an exemplar cause, in which that perfection is contained formally or eminently. One image may indeed be the cause of another image, and that one in turn of another, but still we must arrive at some first exemplar and rest in it, for an infinite progress cannot be admitted here. This rule concerning the exemplar cause of any idea has a notable use in philosophy: for it is the foundation (1) of that demonstration by which we argue from the idea of God for his existence, and (2) of all that certainty which we have from the senses.

units.la: 103. Typos etiam esse rerum futurarum Signa negari nequit, sed dubium est, utrum exemplaribus, an vero imaginibus illi sint annumerandi: ita enim alij Typos vocant rerum futurarum exemplaria, alij imagines potius eos vocant sive umbras rerum futurarum, quemadmodum pictores primas rerum imagines adumbrare ac delineare solent, antequam eas omnibus coloribus suis exornent. Ita magna semper quoad perfectionem est inter Typos & res typis repræsentatas differentia, cùm in typo res rudi tantùm penicillo sit adumbrata.
units.tr: 103. That types are also signs of future things cannot be denied, but it is doubtful whether they are to be counted among exemplars or rather among images. For some call the types exemplars of future things, while others call them rather images, or shadows, of future things, just as painters are accustomed to sketch and outline the first images of things before they adorn them with all their colours. Thus there is always a great difference in perfection between types and the things represented by types, since in the type the thing is only sketched with a rough brush.

units.la: Regulæ de Typis 1. aliæ respiciunt differentiam inter Typum & Antitypum, ut sunt a Quædam dicuntur de Typo, quæ nulla ratione typo, sed antitypo tantùm conveniunt. e. g. Psl. 2. 7. β. Quædam dicuntur de typo, quæ antitypo non conveniunt. y. Non omnia, quæ antitypo conveniunt, typo quoque conveniunt. 2. aliæ respiciunt convenientiam inter Typum & Antitypum, quarum generalissima est: Quædam & typo & antitypo insunt: sed ea tamen, quæ typo & antitypo conveniunt, sunt in duplici differentia. 1. Sunt enim, quæ diversa planè ratione tribuuntur Typo & Antitypo. 2. Sunt etiam quædam, quæ ex eadem ratione tribuuntur, sed gradu tamen diverso. De typis etiam hæc duo notanda. 1. Quod Typus & Antitypus sæpè eandem rem significet. e. g. 1. Pet. 3. 21. Baptismus vocatur aquæ antitypus, quamvis & ipse figura sit. 2. Quod vox Antitypi aliquando pro typo sumatur. e. g. Heb. 9. 24. Apostolus tabernaculum vocat cœlorum Antitypum.
units.tr: The rules concerning types are as follows. 1. Some concern the difference between type and antitype, namely: (a) Some things are said of the type which apply in no way to the type but only to the antitype, e.g. Psl. 2. 7. (b) Some things are said of the type which do not apply to the antitype. (c) Not everything that applies to the antitype also applies to the type. 2. Others concern the agreement between type and antitype, the most general of which is this: Some things belong both to the type and to the antitype, but those things which belong to both type and antitype are of two kinds. (1) For there are things which are attributed to the type and the antitype in a completely different way. (2) There are also some things which are attributed in the same way, but to a different degree. Two things are also to be noted about types. (1) That type and antitype often signify the same thing, e.g. 1 Pet. 3. 21, where baptism is called the antitype of water, although it too is a figure. (2) That the word antitype is sometimes taken for the type, e.g. Heb. 9. 24, where the Apostle calls the tabernacle the antitype of the heavens.

units.la: y. Non omnia, quæ antitypo conveniunt, typo quoque conveniunt.
units.tr: (c) Not everything that applies to the antitype also applies to the type.

units.la: ONTOSOPHIA SPECIALIS
units.tr: ONTOSOPHIA SPECIALIS

units.la: De Generalissimis Entis Divisionibus ac Speciebus.
units.tr: On the Most General Divisions and Species of Being.

units.la: I. QUamvis non uno modo Ens distribuant Metaphysici, nobis tamen Omne Ens est 1. vel Intellectuale vel Materiale. 2. vel Actuale vel Potentiale. 3. vel Infinitum vel Finitum. 4. vel Substantia vel Accidens sive Modus. Equidem vulgò non Ens, sed Substantiam in Spiritum & Corpus distinguunt: sed malè, cùm Accidens etiam, quod Substantiæ contradistinguunt, vel Spirituale sit soli spiritui conveniens, vel Materiale sive corporeum non nisi solis corporibus tribuendum; Ens ergò Intellectuale ita nobis definiendum, ut ejus definitio non tantum substantiæ cogitanti, sed varijs etiam cogitantis substantiæ modis conveniat. Ita Ens Intellectuale est Ens, quod cogitationem in suo conceptu involvit: E contrario Ens Materiale est Ens, quod Extensionem in suo conceptu involvit, vel quod sine Extensione in longum, latum & profundum concipi nequit.
units.tr: I. Although the metaphysicians do not all divide Being in the same way, for us every Being is either (1) Intellectual or Material; (2) Actual or Potential; (3) Infinite or Finite; (4) Substance or Accident, or Mode. Indeed, common usage divides not Being but Substance into Spirit and Body, but this is wrong. The Accident, which they set against Substance, is either spiritual, belonging only to spirit, or material, that is corporeal, to be attributed only to bodies. Therefore Intellectual Being must be defined by us so that its definition applies not only to a thinking substance but also to the various modes of a thinking substance. Thus Intellectual Being is Being that involves thought in its concept. On the contrary, Material Being is Being that involves extension in its concept, or that cannot be conceived without extension in length, breadth and depth.

units.la: Ens Intellectuale vulgò dicitur simplex, invisibile, incorruptibile & immortale. Ens verò materiale & corporeum compositum, divisibile & corruptibile vocatur. Simplex vocatur Ens Intellectuale, non quod nulla planè compositio in eo locum habeat, sed quia non est compositum ex partibus realiter à se invicem distinctis & extra partes positis. Ens verò materiale compositum vocatur, quia partes suas habet, ex quibus est compositum. Invisibile autem vocatur Ens intellectuale, quia, quod corporeum non est, nec visum, nec alios sensus afficere potest: Improprie ergò & de symbolis tantùm externis intelligenda sunt, quæ de spirituum apparitionibus narrantur. Incorruptibile est Ens Intellectuale, non quoad varios cogitandi modos, in quibus varia-
units.tr: The Intellectual Being is commonly called simple, invisible, incorruptible and immortal. But material and corporeal Being is called compound, divisible and corruptible. The Intellectual Being is called simple, not because there is no composition at all in it, but because it is not compounded of parts really distinct from one another and set outside each other. The material Being is called compound because it has parts of which it is made up. It is called invisible because what is not corporeal can neither be seen nor affect the other senses. These terms must therefore be understood improperly, and only of the external symbols that are reported in accounts of the appearances of spirits. The Intellectual Being is incorruptible not with respect to its various modes of thinking, in which variation can take place in more than one way,

units.la: variatio non uno modo locum habere potest, sed quoad substantiæ cogitantis essentiam & existentiam, quæ nec generari, nec corrumpi potest: Generatio autem & corruptio Enti Materiali non tribuitur quoad substantiam sive materiam, sed quoad formam, quæ in variorum modorum complexione consistit. Immortale vocatur Ens Intellectuale, respectu substantiæ, cujus vita in perpetuo cogitandi actu consistit: Sed vita corporea, cùm in varia tantum partium configuratione & motu consistat, mutari potest.
units.tr: but with respect to the essence and existence of the thinking substance, which can be neither generated nor corrupted. Generation and corruption are attributed to material Being not with respect to its substance or matter, but with respect to its form, which consists in a combination of various modes. The Intellectual Being is called immortal with respect to its substance, whose life consists in a perpetual act of thinking. But bodily life, since it consists only in a varying arrangement and motion of parts, can be changed.

units.la: Sunt, qui Ens Reale distinguunt in illud, quod est merè actuale, & in illud quod est partim potentiale, partim actuale, & in illud quod est merè potentiale. Nobis Ens omne est vel Actuale vel Potentiale. Ens Actuale est illud, quod actu existit. Ens vero Potentiale est illud, quod actu quidem non existit, sed tamen potest existere: vocatur etiam Ens potentiâ, unde entia quæ actu non existunt, sed realiter existere possunt, in potentia objectiva esse dicuntur. Deus est ens merè actuale, quia est actus purissimus, in quem nulla cadit potentia, quæ imperfectionem aliquam arguat, nam actu ipso est, quicquid esse potest. Removenda ergò est à Deo. 1. Potentia objectiva, quæ est rei producibilitas à suis causis.
units.tr: Some distinguish Real Being into that which is purely actual, that which is partly potential and partly actual, and that which is purely potential. For us every Being is either Actual or Potential. Actual Being is that which exists in act. Potential Being is that which does not indeed exist in act, but yet can exist; it is also called Being in potency, and so beings that do not exist in act but can really exist are said to be in objective potency. God is purely actual Being, because he is the purest act, into which no potency falls that would argue some imperfection, for he is in act whatever he can be. Therefore the following must be removed from God: (1) objective potency, which is the producibility of a thing from its causes;

units.la: 2. Potentia passiva. 3. Potentia ad non esse. Sed Deo tribui potest Potentia activa, quæ virtutis potiùs vel facultatis, quàm potentiæ nomen meretur: in creaturis quidem potentia activa sæpè imperfectior est suo actu; sed Deus non meliùs aut perfectiùs se habet cùm agit, quàm cùm non agit, in quo voluntas & potentia non differunt, nec proprié Dei potentia, quæ eadem semper est, sed ipsa creatura in actum deducitur: unde Deus etiam ante creationem fuit actuosissimus.
units.tr: (2) passive potency; (3) potency to non-being. But active potency can be attributed to God, though it deserves the name of virtue or faculty rather than of potency. In creatures, indeed, active potency is often more imperfect than its act. But God does not stand better or more perfectly when he acts than when he does not act, in which will and potency do not differ, nor is it properly God's potency, which is always the same, but the creature itself that is brought into act. Hence God was also most active even before creation.

units.la: 4. Omne Ens actuale creatum constat ex actu & potentia. 1.
