Quia in eo varia compositio locum habet, scilicet ex genere & differentia, ex materia & forma, ex essentia & existentia, ex essentia, existentia & subsistentia, ex subjecto & accidente &c. Sed ubi est ejusmodi compositio, ibi unum est principium potentiale sive potentia, & alterum actuale & perfectivum, quod actus dicitur. 2. Quia nullum est ens finitum, in quo non triplex illa potentia imperfectionem arguens locum habeat. Ens potentiâ Metaphysici vulgò intermedium faciunt inter Ens Reale & Nihil, & volunt tale esse ens, quod essentiam quidem habeat, sed existentiam non habeat. e. g. Rosa in hyeme. Nobis Ens potentiâ est merum nihil & non-ens 1. Quia ens potentia est ens, quomodo potentiâ doctus est doctus. 2. Quia mundus non suisset alias creatus ex nihilo, nam suisset ens potentiâ. 3. Quia alias aliquid esset extra Deum, quod non esset productum.
units.tr: (4) Every created actual being consists of act and potency. (1) Because in it there is a manifold composition, namely of genus and differentia, of matter and form, of essence and existence, of essence, existence and subsistence, of subject and accident, and so on. But where there is such a composition, there is one principle that is potential, or potency, and another that is actual and perfective, which is called act. (2) Because there is no finite being in which that threefold potency, which argues imperfection, does not occur. The metaphysicians commonly make being in potency an intermediate between Real Being and Nothing, and want it to be a being that indeed has an essence but does not have existence, as for example a rose in winter. For us being in potency is pure nothing and non-being: (1) because being in potency is being in the way that a man is learned by virtue of learning; (2) because otherwise the world would not have been created out of nothing, for it would have been a being in potency; (3) because otherwise something would exist outside God that had not been produced.

units.la: §. Ens potentia & impossibile sive purum nihil inter se non differunt realiter, si spectentur absolute & in se, quia utrumque in se nihil est: sed differunt connotative, quia unum connotat potentiam productivam, alterum ejusdem potentiæ productivæ negationem connotat: Potentia autem productiva se non potest extendere ad ea, quae impossibilia sunt, quia vel naturae Dei vel naturae rerum a Deo constitutae repugnant. Res autem possibilis vocatur, quia Deus sine sui abnegatione vel mutatione naturae rem illam producere potest. Ergo possibile & impossibile non sunt contradictoria, quia non est oppositio eodem respectu, & in contradictoriis unum entis, alterum non entis est symbolum, & vero utrumque hic est non ens. Ens autem potentia & ens actu catenus differunt, quatenus diversarum rerum existentiam actualē notant: Ens potentiā notat existentiam actualem potentiae, cujus beneficio res potest existere.
units.tr: §. Being in potency and the impossible, or pure nothing, do not differ really from one another if they are considered absolutely and in themselves, because each in itself is nothing. But they differ connotatively, because one connotes a productive potency, while the other connotes the negation of that same productive potency. A productive potency, however, cannot extend itself to things that are impossible, because they are repugnant either to the nature of God or to the nature of things established by God. A thing is called possible, however, because God can produce it without denying himself or changing nature. Therefore possible and impossible are not contradictories, since there is no opposition in the same respect, and in contradictories one term is the sign of being and the other of non-being, whereas both here are non-being. Being in potency and being in act differ only insofar as they denote the actual existence of different things: being in potency denotes the actual existence of a potency by the benefit of which a thing can exist.

units.la: 6. Ens Infinitum est illud, quod nullis omninò terminis circumscriptum est, quale proprie loquendo est solus Deus, qui nullos nec perfectionis, nec durationis, nec extensionis terminos agnoscit, quin imò perfectiones non in se tantum sed & numero infinitas possidet, & nulla est perfectio absolutè talis, quae Deo non conveniat: ita ratione perse-
units.tr: 6. Infinite Being is that which is bounded by no limits at all, which strictly speaking is God alone, who acknowledges no limits of perfection, duration or extension. Indeed, he possesses perfections that are infinite not only in themselves but also in number, and there is no perfection that is absolutely such that does not belong to God. Thus, with respect to

units.la: perfectionis ens infinitum est solus Deus: idem quoq; solus ens infinitum est ratione durationis, quia solus nullum nec principium nec finem, nec durationis successionem admittit: Omnia alia entia existendi principium & successionem habent, & si quæ sunt entia præter Deum, quæ nullum durationis finem habent, duratio tamen illorum non est absolutè necessaria, sed contingens duntaxat, & à Dei conservatione dependet. Ratione extensionis Deus est infinitus, non quòd essentia Dei extensa vel diffusa sit, sed quia Deus est immensus & omni præsens, nullo loco circumscribitur, quia nullus est locus, qui non à Deo conservetur, nec etiam Dei operatio ad locum ita est restricta, ac si nonnisi in loco operari posset Deus, cùm ens fuisset actuosissimum, si vel nullus fuisset mundus, nullus locus. Ens finitum est quod suis terminis circumscribitur.
units.tr: perfection, the only infinite Being is God. Likewise, God alone is an infinite Being with respect to duration, because he alone admits neither beginning nor end nor succession of duration. All other beings have a beginning of existence and succession. And if there are any beings besides God that have no end of duration, nevertheless their duration is not absolutely necessary but merely contingent, and depends on God's preservation. With respect to extension God is infinite, not because the essence of God is extended or diffused, but because God is immense and present to all things, and is circumscribed by no place, since there is no place that is not preserved by God. Nor is God's operation so restricted to place, as if God could act only in a place; he would have been most active even if there had been no world and no place. A finite Being is that which is circumscribed by its own limits.

units.la: 7. Recentiores nonnulli Infinitum vocant illud, quod nullos plane terminos habet, quodque nulla plane relimitatum est, ut Deus. Indefinitum vero vocant illud, quod in se quidem finitum & terminatum est, sed cujus terminos nos ignoramus: ita dicunt, Mundum esse indefinitæ magnitudinis quoad nos, corpus esse divisibile in indefinitum, quia ultima pars, in quam dividi potest à nobis ignoratur: & tale vulgò Infinitum Syncategorematicum vocant, h. e. non tot quin plura. Alij inter Infinitum perfectione & inter Infinitum mole distinguunt, quemadmodum finitudo alia est virtutis sive perfectionis, alia molis sive corporis: Infinitudo perfectionis est in ente summè perfecto, cujus perfectiones nullo modo nec in se nec quoad numerum sunt limitatæ. Infinitudo vero molis si quæ daretur, non ideo tamen summè persecta foret, ita ut si vel maximè quoad molem infinitus statueretur Mundus, nullum tamen esset periculum, ne mundus quoad perfectionem finitus semper agnosceretur. Non possunt quidem esse duo infinita ejusdem generis, non possunt esse duo Dij infiniti & summè perfecti: non possunt esse se duo mundi infiniti, sed ut aliud sit infinitum virtute, aliud infinitum mole nullam implicat contradictionem.
units.tr: 7. Some more recent writers call infinite that which has no limits at all, and which is not limited in any way, as God is. They call indefinite that which is indeed finite and bounded in itself, but whose bounds we do not know. Thus they say the world is of indefinite magnitude as far as we are concerned, and that a body is divisible into an indefinite number of parts, because we do not know the last part into which it can be divided. Such a thing is commonly called syncategorematically infinite, that is, not so many that there could not be more. Others distinguish between infinity of perfection and infinity of mass, just as finitude is one thing of power or perfection and another of mass or body. The infinity of perfection is in the supremely perfect being, whose perfections are in no way limited, either in themselves or in number. The infinity of mass, if it were to exist, would not on that account be supremely perfect; so even if the world were posited as infinite in mass, there would be no danger that the world would not always be recognised as finite in perfection. Indeed there cannot be two infinite things of the same kind, there cannot be two infinite and supremely perfect gods, and there cannot be two infinite worlds. But that one thing should be infinite in power and another infinite in mass implies no contradiction.

units.la: 8. Verum Nos distinguimus inter Metaphysicam & Physicam, inter Ens & Corpus: In Metaphysica omne Ens est vel Infinitum vel Finitum, in Physica omne Corpus est vel Indefinitum vel Finitum. Ens Infinitum est, cujus perfectiones non sunt limitatæ: quale infinitum est solus Deus. Ens Finitum est, cujus perfectiones sunt limitatæ: qualis finitudo competit omnibus creaturis, etiam toti mundo. Corpus Finitum est, cujus magnitudo est limitata & determinata. Corpus vero Indefinitum vocatur, cujus limites vel ultimas partes cogitare implicat contradictionem: talis indefinitudo est in magnitudine totius universi, cujus limites & extremas partes non tantum ignoramus, sed eas nequidem sine contradictione cogitare possumus: talis etiam indefinitudo est in divisibilitate materiæ, cujus pars ultima, quæ indivisibilis sit, & nullas amplius partes habeat, sine contradictione cogitari nequit: ita nomen etiam Infiniti soli Deo reservamus.
units.tr: 8. But we distinguish between Metaphysics and Physics, and between Being and Body. In Metaphysics every Being is either Infinite or Finite; in Physics every Body is either Indefinite or Finite. An Infinite Being is one whose perfections are not limited, and this kind of infinity belongs to God alone. A Finite Being is one whose perfections are limited, and this kind of finitude belongs to all creatures, even to the whole world. A Finite Body is one whose magnitude is limited and determined. An Indefinite Body, however, is one whose limits or ultimate parts it is self-contradictory to think of. Such indefiniteness is found in the magnitude of the whole universe, whose limits and outermost parts we not only do not know but cannot even think of without contradiction. Such indefiniteness is also found in the divisibility of matter, whose ultimate part, one that is indivisible and has no further parts, cannot be thought of without contradiction. So we reserve the name Infinite for God alone.

units.la: 9. Ens Infinitum variis etiam aliis nominibus indigitari solet: nam 1. vocatur Ens Increatum contradistincte ad Ens Creatum, quale est omne ens finitum: nam quod infinite perfectum est, hanc etiam perfectionem habet, ut sit a se nec sit ab alio productum: Id enim quod limitatas habet persectiones, a se esse nequit, sed necessario ab alio productum & creatum est; nam si a se esset, perfectiones sibi dedisset illimitatas: unde finitum esse & creatum esse ejusdem sunt latitudinis.
units.tr: 9. Infinite Being is also commonly designated by various other names. First, it is called Uncreated Being, in contrast to Created Being, which is every finite being. For what is infinitely perfect has this perfection too, that it is from itself and is not produced by another. For that which has limited perfections cannot be from itself, but is necessarily produced and created by another; for if it were from itself, it would have given itself unlimited perfections. Hence being finite and being created have the same range.

units.la: 2. Vocatur Ens Independens, quia dependere ab aliquo imperfectionem aliquam dicit: unde omnis creatura vocatur Ens Dependens, quia a Deo tanquam a Creatore suo & quoad essentiam & quoad existentiam dependet.
units.tr: 2. It is called Independent Being, because to depend on something says that there is some imperfection. Hence every creature is called Dependent Being, because it depends on God as its Creator, both in its essence and in its existence.

units.la: 10. 3. Vocatur Ens Necessarium, quia non potest non existere: Ens enim summe perfectum non existere, implicat contradictionem: Sed Ens finitum & Creatum est Ens Contingens, quia ita existit, ut possit non existere, quemadmodum etiam aliquando non fuit.
units.tr: 10. 3. It is called Necessary Being, because it cannot not exist: for it is self-contradictory that a supremely perfect Being should not exist. But a finite and created being is a Contingent Being, because it exists in such a way that it could not exist, just as it also at some time did not exist.

units.la: 4. Vocatur Ens à se, non negative tantum, quatenus non est ab alio, sed etiam positive, quatenus ratio formalis, propter quam nulla causa indiget, quam maximè positiva est, summa scilicet & infinita Dei perfectio.
units.tr: 4. It is called Being from itself, not merely negatively, insofar as it is not from another, but also positively, insofar as its formal reason, on account of which it needs no cause, is most positive, namely the highest and infinite perfection of God.

units.la: 5. Vocatur Ens per essentiam tale, quia existentia est de Dei essentia: Sed omnia reliqua entia finita sunt à Deo & à causis suis, ac quam habent essentiam & existentiam, aliunde acceperunt: unde Entia per participationem vocantur.
units.tr: 5. It is called Being such through its essence, because existence belongs to the essence of God. But all the other finite beings are from God and from their causes, and they have received from elsewhere both the essence and the existence they possess. Hence they are called Beings through participation.

units.la: 11. Nulla est frequentior Entis distributio, quàm ea, quâ in Substantiam & Accidens vulgò dividitur: quam tamen nonnulli inadæquatam esse volunt, & Modos intermedios faciunt inter Substantiam & Accidens. Nobis autem ea immediata est, nec inter Substantiam & Accidens Ens tertium admittimus, quia non alios hic Modos admittimus, quàm qui Accidentia sunt, nec alia nobis sunt Accidentia, quam quæ modi sunt. Quamvis autem nulla dentur Accidentia Realia, nec Accidentia entia sint à Substantijs realiter distincta, distributio tamen hæc est Entis Realis. Quamvis etiam Ens respectu Substantia & Accidentis non sit genus univocum, nec tamen merè æquivocum est, sed analogum, quia Accidens Substantiæ acceptum refert, quòd Entis naturam participet, cùm Accidentis esse sit inesse substantiæ.
units.tr: 11. No division of Being is more frequent than the one by which it is commonly divided into Substance and Accident. Some, however, hold that this division is inadequate and make Modes intermediate between Substance and Accident. For us, however, this division is immediate, and we do not admit a third kind of being between Substance and Accident, because we admit no other modes here than those that are Accidents, and for us there are no other Accidents than those that are modes. Although no real Accidents are given, and accidents, being beings, are not really distinct from substances, this division is nevertheless a division of Real Being. Although Being with respect to Substance and Accident is not a univocal genus, it is not purely equivocal either, but analogous, because an Accident refers its character to substance, since it shares in the nature of being, the being of an accident being to inhere in a substance.

units.la: 12. Substantia vox a mbigua est: nam sumitur 1. pro essentia alicujus rei, quam Græcè οὐσίαν vocant, unde forsan ortæ formæ substantiales. 2. Pro Subjecto, quod substat accidentibus. 3. Pro Substantia actionis, quæ opponitur circumstantijs. 4. Pro Suppositio, quod est substantia singularis ultimò completa, ut postea videbimus. 5. Pro ea Entis specie, quæ opponitur Accidenti: & hoc ultimo sensu Substantia vulgò definitur Ens Per se subsistens: sed hæc definitio ambigua est propter vocis subsistendi ambiguitatem: nam per se subsistere aliquando idem est quod per se existere, h. e. nulla plane alia re opus habere ad existendum: sed quia sic solus Deus esset substantia per se & a se existens, per se subsistere in definitione substantiae significat non existere in alio tanquam in Subjecto, quamvis alteri per modum partis vel alio aliquo modo inesse posiit, & ita per se subsistere convenit omni substantiae, cujus formale est Subsistentia: sed aliquando Subsistentia & subsistendi vox strictissime sumitur pro peculiari subsistendi modo, qui convenit supposito: ita ut inter existentiam, subsistentiam late & subsistentiam stricte sumptam haec sit differentia, quod existentia omni enti, Subsistentia late sumpta omni substantiae & Subsistentia stricte sumpta soli supposito conveniat.
units.tr: 12. The word Substance is ambiguous. For it is taken: 1. for the essence of a thing, which the Greeks call ousia [οὐσία], whence perhaps the so-called substantial forms arose; 2. for the Subject, which underlies accidents; 3. for the substance of an action, which is opposed to its circumstances; 4. for the Suppositum, which is a singular substance ultimately complete, as we shall see later; 5. for that kind of being which is opposed to Accident. And in this last sense Substance is commonly defined as Being subsisting per se. But this definition is ambiguous because of the ambiguity of the word subsisting. For to subsist per se sometimes means the same as to exist per se, that is, to need no other thing at all in order to exist. But if that were so, God alone would be a substance existing per se and from itself. So in the definition of substance, to subsist per se means not to exist in another as in a subject, although it may be in another as a part or in some other way. In this sense to subsist per se belongs to every substance, whose formal character is subsistence. But sometimes subsistence and to subsist are taken most strictly, for a particular mode of subsisting that belongs to a suppositum. So between existence, subsistence taken broadly and subsistence taken strictly there is this difference: existence belongs to every being, subsistence taken broadly belongs to every substance, and subsistence taken strictly belongs only to a suppositum.

units.la: 13. Rectius alij Substantiam definiunt ens, quod nulla alia re creata indiget ad existendum: vel, quod in existendo a nulla alia re creata dependet. Eam Metaphysici vulgo distinguunt 1. in Infinitam & Finitam. 2. in Primam & Secundam. 3. in Completam & Incompletam, & 4. in Cogitantem & Extensam sive Spiritum & Corpus. Sed cùm de Infinito & Finito antea actum fuerit in distributione entis, cùm de Spiritu Noëtica agat & de Corpore Somatica, secunda demùm & tertia distinctio hujus est loci. Distinctio autem Substantiæ in Primam & Secundam non est generis in suas species, sed analogi in sua analogata, quia prima substantia est magis & prius substantia quàm substantia secunda, h. e. magis & prius est subjectum accidentibus quàm secunda: nam substantia prima est primum subjectum. ejusque gratiâ ac beneficio demùm subjectum fit substantia secunda, unde subjectum secundum vocatur.
units.tr: 13. More correctly, others define Substance as a being that needs no other created thing in order to exist, or that in existing does not depend on any other created thing. Metaphysicians commonly distinguish it: 1. into Infinite and Finite; 2. into First and Second; 3. into Complete and Incomplete; and 4. into Thinking and Extended, or Spirit and Body. But since the infinite and the finite were treated earlier in the division of being, and since the discussion of spirit belongs to noetics and that of body to somatics, only the second and third distinctions belong to this place. The division of Substance into First and Second is not a division of a genus into its species but of an analogue into its analogates. For first substance is more and prior substance than second substance; that is, it is more and prior subject of accidents than the second. For first substance is the primary subject, and for its sake and by its benefit the subject finally becomes second substance, which is why it is called second subject.

units.la: §4. Substantia prima est substantia singularis. e. g. Petrus. Substantia secunda est substantia universalis, e. g. Homo. Substantia ergò prima est individuum, quod habet attributa singularia: Sed Substantia secunda est Genus vel Species, quæ confusè & cum attributis communibus sumitur: Substantiam primam de subjecto nec dici nec subjecto inesse statuunt: Substantiam vero secundam de subjecto quidem dici, sed nulli subjecto inesse statuunt. In Physica Materia prima est materia universalis & in genere considerata, sed materia secunda est materia particularis vel singularis: sed in Metaphysica substantia secunda est substantia universalis multiplicabilis in pluribus inferioribus & individuis, ut Homo. Sed Substantia prima est substantia singularis, non multiplicabilis in pluribus inferioribus vel individuis, e. g. hic homo actu in rerum natura existens.
units.tr: §4. First substance is a singular substance, for example Peter. Second substance is a universal substance, for example Man. So first substance is an individual, which has singular attributes. But second substance is a genus or species, which is taken in a general way and with common attributes. They hold that first substance is neither predicated of a subject nor inheres in a subject, but that second substance is indeed predicated of a subject, yet inheres in no subject. In Physics, prime matter is matter that is universal and considered in general, but secondary matter is particular or singular matter. But in Metaphysics second substance is a universal substance that can be multiplied in many inferiors and individuals, such as Man. And first substance is a singular substance, not multiplicable in many inferiors or individuals, for example this man actually existing in the nature of things.

units.la: §. Distinctio substantia in Incompletam & Completam non respicit ipsam substantiae naturam, quasi quaedam esset substantia, quae omnia ad substantiam requisita non haberet, Incompleta ideo dicenda. Sed Incompleta vocatur substantia, quae ordinata est ad ulteriorem compositionem, quema admodum omnes partes ordinatae sunt ad compositionem totius. Substantia ergo completa vocatur, quae aut totum quid est, aut instar totius concipitur, e. g. Angelus. Substantia vero Incompleta est, quae aut non est totum quid, aut instar totius non concipitur: ita quaelibet pars totius potest vocari Substantia incompleta: ita mens, isa corpus nostrum est Supstantia incompleta: homo vero est substantia completa.
units.tr: §. The division of substance into Incomplete and Complete does not concern the very nature of substance, as if there were some substance lacking all that is required for substance and for that reason to be called Incomplete. Rather, a substance is called Incomplete when it is ordered toward a further composition, just as all parts are ordered toward the composition of a whole. So a complete substance is one that either is a whole thing or is conceived in the manner of a whole, for example an Angel. An incomplete substance, however, is one that either is not a whole thing or is not conceived in the manner of a whole. Thus any part of a whole can be called an incomplete substance: so the mind, and likewise our body, is an incomplete substance, but the human being is a complete substance.

units.la: Sunt qui putant omnem substantiam primam & singularem esse Suppositum, quo sensu dicunt, Actiones esse suppositorum. Sed rectius alij Suppositum à substantia prima distinguunt: nam 1. Essentia Divina, quae communis est tribus personis, est substantia prima & singularis, nec tamen est suppositum. 2. Natura Christi humana est substantia singularis ac prima, nec tamen est Suppositum. 3. In Deo tria sunt supposita, quia tres personae, & tamen una tantum est essentia singularis. 4. In Christo non sunt duo supposita, quia non sunt duae personae, sed tamen duae sunt essentiae seu naturae singulares, divina & humana. Omnis ergo substantia singularis incompleta, vel quae alteri communicatur, aut jam constitutae adjungitur, est substantia prima, sed tamen non est
units.tr: Some hold that every first and singular substance is a suppositum, and in this sense they say that actions belong to supposita. But others more correctly distinguish a suppositum from a first substance. (1) The divine essence, which is common to the three persons, is a first and singular substance, yet it is not a suppositum. (2) The human nature of Christ is a singular and first substance, yet it is not a suppositum. (3) In God there are three supposita, because there are three persons, and yet there is only one singular essence. (4) In Christ there are not two supposita, because there are not two persons, yet there are two singular essences or natures, the divine and the human. Therefore every singular substance that is incomplete, or that is communicated to another, or is joined to one already constituted, is a first substance, but nevertheless is not

units.la: Suppositum ergo est substantia prima & singularis, quæ cum alia non consticuit tertiam substantiam vel naturam substantialem, nec alteri jam constitutæ adjungitur: indè enim oritur peculiaris subsistendi modus, qui barbaro Suppositalitatis nomine venit. Ad Suppositum ergo requiritur 1. Ut sit substantia: Accidens enim cum extra unionem & communicationem cum substantia existere nequeat, Suppositum esse nequit. 2. Ut sit substantia prima & singularis, quia substantia universalis quà talis, e. g. homo in genere non existit. 3. Ut sit substantia, quæ cum alia tertiam naturam substantialem non constituat; partes enim quà tales quia sunt substantiæ incompletæ, non sunt supposita, quamvis sint substantiæ primæ & singulares 4. Ut sit substantia prima & singularis, quæ alteri non communicetur, ita enim essentia divina, quamvis substantia sit prima & singularis, suppositum tamen non est, quia communis est tribus SS. Trinitatis personis. 5. Ut alteri jam constituta non adjungatur: ita enim natura Christi humana na non est suppositum, quamvis sit substantia singularis, quia personæ divinæ unita vel adjuncta est.
units.tr: A suppositum is therefore a first and singular substance which, when combined with another, does not constitute a third substance or substantial nature, and which is not joined to one already constituted. From this arises a peculiar mode of subsisting, which the barbarous term suppositality denotes. Therefore, for a suppositum the following are required. (1) That it be a substance: for an accident cannot exist apart from union and communication with a substance, and so cannot be a suppositum. (2) That it be a first and singular substance, because a universal substance as such, for example man in general, does not exist. (3) That it be a substance which, when combined with another, does not constitute a third substantial nature; for parts as such, since they are incomplete substances, are not supposita, although they are first and singular substances. (4) That it be a first and singular substance which is not communicated to another: thus the divine essence, although it is a first and singular substance, is nevertheless not a suppositum, because it is common to the three persons of the Holy Trinity. (5) That it not be joined to one already constituted: thus the human nature of Christ is not a suppositum, although it is a singular substance, because it is united or joined to the divine person.

units.la: 18. Suppositalitas in non-communicatione consistit sive in sola negatione compositionis & adjunctionis: non autem in incommunicabilitate, si suppositum sit creatum, cùm omni rei creatæ ulterior ordinatio ad aliam rem & ita communicabilitas accedere queat, e.g. particulæ elementares, quousq; seorsim existunt, supposita sunt, & tamen alteri incommunicabiles non sunt, ut videre est in unoquoq; composito sita mens à corpore separata suppositum est æq; ac angelus, quamvis rationem semper partis habere & retinere videatur, quia ratio suppositi in non-communicatione consistit. Non ergo Substantiæ, sed donorum respectu intelligenda est Communicatio & donatio Spiritus Sancti, quem suppositum esse probant actiones, quæ nonnisi suppositis tribui possunt. In Supposito autem Creato modus ille suppositalitatis non est positivum quid & Substantia distinctum, sed mera communicationis negatio. 1. Quia nulla est necessitas statuendi modum positivum, cùm entia non sint multiplicanda citra necessitatem. 2. Si suppositalitas esset modus positivus, toties substantia ipsa mutaretur, quoties fieret vel desineret esse suppositum. 3. Alias Corpora nostra ante & post resurrectionem non essent eadem supposita, quia non foret una & eadem suppositalitas, unus enim idemq; numero modus, postquam semel periit, reproduci nequit. 4. Alias Christus quoad humanam naturam nobis non foret per omnia similis, sed careret modo aliquo positivo: & ita natura ejus humana nostra fuisset imperfectior.
units.tr: 18. Suppositality consists in non-communication, that is, in the mere negation of composition and adjunction; it does not consist in incommunicability, if the suppositum is created, since a further ordering of any created thing to another thing, and so communicability, can be added to it. For example, elementary particles, so long as they exist separately, are supposita, and yet they are not incommunicable to another, as can be seen in every composite. The mind separated from the body is a suppositum just as much as an angel, although it seems always to have and retain the character of a part, because the nature of a suppositum consists in non-communication. Therefore the communication and gift of the Holy Spirit is not to be understood with respect to substance but with respect to gifts; that the Spirit is a suppositum is proved by the actions, which can be attributed only to supposita. In a created Suppositum, however, that mode of suppositality is not something positive and distinct from the substance, but a mere negation of communication. (1) Because there is no necessity to posit a positive mode, since beings are not to be multiplied without necessity. (2) If suppositality were a positive mode, the substance itself would be changed as often as it began or ceased to be a suppositum. (3) Otherwise our bodies before and after the resurrection would not be the same supposita, because there would not be one and the same suppositality; for one and the same mode, numerically, once it has perished, cannot be reproduced. (4) Otherwise Christ, with respect to his human nature, would not be in all things similar to us, but would lack some positive mode, and so his human nature would be more imperfect than ours.

units.la: Sed in Supposito Increato h. e. in personis SS. Trinitatis Suppositalitas superaddit modum positivum. 1. Quia Suppositalitas in divinis est principium operationum ad intra, quemadmodum in rebus creatis Suppositum ex sola natura sua constituitur principium sufficiens omnium suarum operationum : at vero Pater e. g. in S. S. Trinitate non potest dici generare Filium, si praecise habeatur respectus Essentiae, eam enim Pater cum Filio & Spiritu Sancto habet communem. 2. Quia Suppositalitas in divinis est fundamentum distinctionis inter essentiam & personas & inter ipsas personas: nec enim Divinitas praecise sumpta inter Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum, distinguit, quemadmodum Supposita creata hoc solo distinguuntur, quòd numero differant.
units.tr: But in an uncreated Suppositum, that is, in the persons of the Holy Trinity, suppositality adds a positive mode. (1) Because suppositality in the divine persons is the principle of operations ad intra; just as in created things the suppositum, constituted by its nature alone, is a sufficient principle of all its operations. Yet the Father, for example in the Holy Trinity, cannot be said to beget the Son if regard is had merely to the essence, for the Father has the essence in common with the Son and the Holy Spirit. (2) Because suppositality in the divine persons is the ground of the distinction between the essence and the persons, and among the persons themselves. For the Godhead, taken merely as such, does not distinguish the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; whereas created supposita are distinguished by this alone, that they differ in number.

units.la: 2o. Omnis Persona est Suppositum: sed non omne Suppositum est Persona. Persona autem est Suppositum intelligens. Quamvis enim vox Personae proprie significet larvam, & ideò in Comoedijs potissimum vox illa fuerit usurpata, usu tamen translata est ad significandam substantiam singularem intelligentem: in specie autem vox haec translata fuit ad mysterium SS. Trinitatis, ubi Graeci tres hypostases, Latini tres personas agnoverunt. Hic autem vox Persona non tàm significat substantiam singularem, quàm modum subsistendi. substantiæ singularis: aliâs in divinis statuendæ sorent tres substantiæ singulares, cùm tamen tres personæ hîc significent tres modos subsistendi unius ejusdemq; substantiæ singularis, scilicet essentiæ divinæ. Ubi ergò tres sunt personæ, ibi vel tres sunt substantiæ singulares, ut in rebus creatis Petrus, Paulus & Johannes: vel tres sunt modi subsistendi unius ejusdemq; substantiæ singularis, ut in divinis Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus.
units.tr: 2. Every person is a suppositum, but not every suppositum is a person. A person, however, is an intelligent suppositum. For although the word persona properly signifies a mask, and for that reason was chiefly used in comedies, yet by usage it has been transferred to signify an intelligent singular substance. In particular, this word was transferred to the mystery of the Holy Trinity, where the Greeks acknowledged three hypostases and the Latins three persons. Here, however, the word person signifies not so much a singular substance as a mode of subsisting of a singular substance; otherwise three singular substances would have to be posited in the divine nature, whereas the three persons here signify three modes of subsisting of one and the same singular substance, namely the divine essence. Where there are three persons, therefore, there are either three singular substances, as in created things Peter, Paul and John; or there are three modes of subsisting of one and the same singular substance, as in the divine nature the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 21. Persona est vel Increata vel Creata, Persona increata sunt tres: Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus. Persona autem creata est vel Angelica vel Humana. Duplex autem est personam definiendi modus, vel in abstracto vel in concreto: cùm enim in SS. Trinitate triplex Persona tribuitur Deo, Persona vox in abstracto sumitur, non in concreto, & proindè non significat triplicem substantiam singularem intelligentem, sed unius substantiæ singularis intelligentis, essentiæ scilicet divinæ, triplicem subsistendi modum. dum. Sed Persona sumitur in concreto, cum de rebus creatis dicitur sive Angelis sive Hominibus, & significat substantiam singularem intelligentem: unde multiplicatis personis multiplicantur etiam substantiæ. Sed in divinis modi tantum subsistendi multiplicantur: nam omnis quidem persona habet singularem essentiam, sed non omnis persona essentiam habet singularem & separatam, in divinis enim plures sunt personæ in una eademᶃ; essentia singulari. Quinimo ipsi quoq; Theologi Personas divinas vel in abstracto vel in concreto definire solent: ita enim Personæ divinæ in abstracto sunt subsistentiæ quædam in essentia divina proprietatibus incommunicabilibus distinctæ: in concreto autem Personæ divinæ sunt substantiæ sive supposita incommunicabiliter distincta.
units.tr: 21. A person is either uncreated or created. The uncreated persons are three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. A created person is either angelic or human. There is a twofold way of defining a person, either in the abstract or in the concrete. For since in the Holy Trinity a threefold Person is attributed to God, the word person is taken in the abstract and not in the concrete, and so it does not signify three intelligent singular substances, but the threefold mode of subsisting of one intelligent singular substance, namely the divine essence. But person is taken in the concrete when it is said of created things, whether of angels or of men, and it signifies an intelligent singular substance; hence with the multiplying of persons the substances are also multiplied. But in the divine nature only the modes of subsisting are multiplied; for every person indeed has a singular essence, yet not every person has a singular and separate essence, for in the divine nature there are several persons in one and the same singular essence. Indeed the theologians themselves are accustomed to define the divine Persons either in the abstract or in the concrete. Thus the divine Persons in the abstract are certain subsistences in the divine essence distinguished by incommunicable properties; but in the concrete the divine Persons are substances or supposita incommunicably distinct.

units.tr: Come, my dear Rudolph, tested and approved. Flourish, O mine, happy now in all things, let nothing be nothing. May Hercules' labour be in the Lord; may he repel the weapons, and so with good omens may he destroy all of them with the sword. Now let the Muses sing great praises and proclaim great triumphs. Your fame is fine. Flourish! May God preserve you, and may Jehovah further these undertakings.

units.la: ROscidus hicce RODOLPH virtute virescit in agris, Grandia cum peragit, rore, virore viret: Otia dum vitat, virgulta virida quaerit, Recte facit, studijs invigilare suis Dum cupit, iste studet pretium persolvere Musis Unde venit, GRUNER scandere quod Cathedram Optatam possit, celso de ponte Cathedra Eruit hic hostes, destruit atque fugat. Ludando VULPES HORRENDAS pelle vel URGE, NON parcas, O! HIS, ne capiaris ab his; Praemia sunt praesto certantibus, ac manet ipsos Eximium nomen, gloria, magnus honos. Hoc clarum specimen, quod GRUNER grunet aperte Rem probat esse bonam, nomen & omen adest.
units.tr: This dewy Rudolph flourishes in the fields with virtue; when he carries out great deeds, he grows green with dew and greenness. While he avoids idleness, he seeks green shoots. He does well to keep watch over his studies, and while he desires it, he takes pains to pay his dues to the Muses. Hence it comes that Gruner can climb to the coveted chair; from the high bridge the chair snatches up enemies and routs and puts them to flight. In play, drive off or urge on the dreadful foxes; do not spare, O, these, lest you be caught by them. Rewards are ready for those who strive, and an outstanding name, glory and great honour await them. This clear specimen, which Gruner grunts openly, proves the thing to be good, and the name is also an omen.

units.tr: He who sets before himself the straight course to the goal he has proposed keeps vigil over his studies; whoever wants to reach the goal wishes to spare no labour, for the rewards of virtue await the worthy. Zeal urges him to follow the whole company of scholars and to turn over the learned writings of learned men. Indeed, dear Rudolph, you now rightly [ὀρθῶς] turn these matters over in your mind, and you teach doctrine clearly and plainly. Now your mind is set to defend these theses from the Chair; with a cheerful spirit, repel the weapons of your enemies. May almighty God graciously favour you, and may the ninefold choir prepare an outstanding palm. Always press on to climb the mountain of the Muses; from there honour and virtue, glory and praise flow forth. A. A. A. A. Rare are the verdant places of the Pierides, which display the fruits of Phoebus' most celebrated nursling. Here dense garlands are heaped up, and wisdom adorns the choir of the Thespiads [the Muses] with the laurels of Apollo. Now Phoebus binds the victor's temples; on Parnassus and by the green Vireto [Viretus] it is played: the undying praise of Hector's [Rudolph's] distinguished sons.

units.la: Respice non torvo Parnasia munera vultu, Gratulor ex animo Carmine namque tibi: Omnia sic cedant feliciter omine laeto, Robore teque suo roboret Omnipotens Deiicias hostes, doctrinae pondere sternas, Ut nobis vivas laetus honore tuo: O! per te nomen magnum, sic gloria surget Nomen in orbe tuum semper erit celebre, Laudes ipse tuas extendam ego ad astra polumque: Exclamabo: Omnes nunc celebrate meum Pectore, quem socium longo cognoscitis usu, Res bene succedat: Carmina laetum ego, Haecce Georg Hollard scripsi Sophiae Studiosus, Us u quem poteris semper habere tuum.
units.tr: Do not look on these Parnassian gifts with a scowling face; I congratulate you from my heart, for I sing this poem to you. May all things turn out happily under a joyful omen, and may Almighty God strengthen you with his own strength, that you may crush your enemies with the weight of your learning, and live happily for us with your honour intact. O, through you the great name, thus glory will rise; your name will always be famous in the world. I myself will extend your praises to the stars and the sky, and cry out: "Now all of you celebrate this with your heart, you whom you know as a companion through long experience. May the affair turn out well; I write these songs gladly." I, Georg Hollard, a student of wisdom, have written these lines, which you will always be able to have as your own.
